questions.question: As an L1 analyst you notice that one detection rule fires about 300 times a day, and every alert from it in the last three weeks was closed as benign because it matches the same scheduled backup job. What should you do?

options.text: Close new alerts from this rule in bulk without opening them, since the pattern is already known and documented
Keep triaging each alert individually, because tuning rules is not part of the L1 role
Send the rule owner a tuning request with example alerts, the repeating fields and how you verified the backup
Disable the rule in the SIEM yourself so that the queue becomes manageable again

explanation.correct: Repeated benign alerts from one cause are a tuning problem, and the analyst who sees them first holds the evidence. A useful tuning request lists example alerts, the fields that are identical every time (for example the backup service account, the host and the parent process) and how you confirmed the activity is the scheduled backup. The rule owner can then add a narrow exception, for example in Microsoft Sentinel through a watchlist referenced by the rule or an automation rule that expires, which removes the noise without blinding the rule to other activity.

distractors.a: Bulk-closing without opening is how real incidents get missed: an attacker using the same host or account would be closed together with the noise, and the noise stays for the next shift.
distractors.b: Triaging the same benign pattern 300 times a day is the cause of alert fatigue, not the cure. L1 is expected to report repeating patterns so they can be fixed at the rule.
distractors.d: Disabling a production rule is a change the rule owner makes through change control, not an L1 action, and it would also remove detection of the malicious cases the rule exists for.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you treat noise as something to report and fix with evidence, rather than something to absorb silently or switch off.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Handle false positives in Microsoft Sentinel

questions.question: In a bank's SOC, the same 'suspicious service installation' rule fires at the same moment on a payment-processing server and on a training-room PC. Both alerts carry the rule's default severity, Medium. Why does the queue rank the payment-server alert higher?

options.text: Priority weighs rule severity together with asset criticality, and the payment server is far more critical
Detections on servers are more reliable than on workstations, so that alert is more likely to be a true positive
The rule's severity is set wrongly and should be raised to High for every host it runs on
The payment server is in regulatory scope, so every alert on it must be reported to the regulator

explanation.correct: A rule author cannot know which host a detection will fire on, so rule severity describes the behaviour, while queue priority also weighs context such as asset criticality, account privilege and exposure. The same behaviour on a payment server threatens a critical service and customer funds; on a training PC it still needs checking but can wait behind the critical asset. SIEMs support this with asset or entity context, for example a Microsoft Sentinel watchlist of high-value assets used in the rule or in an automation rule that raises severity.

distractors.b: The host type does not change how accurate the rule is; its fidelity is the same on both machines. The ranking reflects impact, not likelihood.
distractors.c: Raising severity everywhere would also push the training-room PC up and inflate the whole queue. The fix is context-based priority, not a blanket change to the rule.
distractors.d: An alert is not a reportable incident. Regulatory reporting (for example under DORA) applies to incidents classified as major, after analysis, not to every alert on an in-scope system.

explanation.interview_angle: Checks that you separate what the rule saw (severity) from what it means to this business (priority).

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Watchlists in Microsoft Sentinel
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

questions.question: Your bank's runbook gives L1 30 minutes to triage a High alert. At minute 25 you still cannot tell whether a login to the internet-banking admin portal from a new country is legitimate. What do you do?

options.text: Close it as benign so the SLA is met, and reopen it later if new information appears
Set the alert to 'in progress' so the SLA clock stops, and continue when the queue is quieter
Keep investigating past the SLA without telling anyone, since an accurate verdict matters more than the clock
Escalate to L2 as the runbook allows, with notes on what you checked and what is still unknown

explanation.correct: An SLA promises that an alert gets the right level of attention in time; it is not a deadline to produce a verdict at any cost. When L1 triage cannot reach a conclusion within the window, the runbook path is to escalate with notes: what you checked (sign-in details, device, MFA result, the user's usual locations), what you found and what is still open. L2 then starts from your work, and a possibly compromised admin session is not left waiting.

distractors.a: Closing an unresolved High alert as benign to beat a timer is exactly how metrics end up hiding real incidents, and the closure is recorded with a wrong classification.
distractors.b: Changing the status to stop the clock games the metric while nobody actually works the alert; the risk stays open and the report becomes misleading.
distractors.c: Overrunning silently means nobody senior knows a possible admin compromise is open. Accuracy matters, but the answer is a documented handover, not holding the alert past its window.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

questions.question: A bank's SOC measures 'mean time to detect' from the moment the SIEM creates an alert until an analyst acknowledges it, and reports 8 minutes. True or false: this lets the CISO tell the board that intrusions are detected within about 8 minutes of the attacker's first action.

options.text: True
False

explanation.correct: False. The clock starts when the SIEM creates the alert, so the figure measures how quickly the queue is picked up, which is really a time-to-acknowledge. It says nothing about the gap between the attacker's first action and the alert: an intrusion that went unnoticed for weeks before a rule fired still scores 8 minutes, and intrusions that never trigger a rule are not counted at all. Dwell time is established afterwards, during investigation, from the earliest evidence of compromise. A board report should state exactly what each timer measures and include intrusions found by other means (hunting, testing, third parties).

distractors.a: Accepting the number as stated confuses queue pick-up speed with detection speed; the clock only starts after the hardest part, detecting the activity at all, has already happened.

explanation.interview_angle: Can you explain what a metric actually measures before it is shown to senior management?

references.title: NIST SP 800-55 Vol. 1: Measurement Guide for Information Security

questions.question: Six months after a bank's SOC added mean time to resolve (MTTR) to analysts' individual performance goals, MTTR fell from 4 hours to 40 minutes. Over the same period the incident reopen rate tripled, and a quality review found many closures with no evidence recorded. Alert volume and tooling did not change. What is the most likely explanation and the right response?

options.text: Analysts became far more efficient; the reopen rate rose because users now report more issues, so nothing needs to change
Clock drift on the SIEM is distorting durations, so MTTR should be recalculated before any conclusion is drawn
Experience made investigations genuinely faster, and the higher reopen rate is an unrelated problem to look at separately
Analysts are closing early to hit the target; balance MTTR with quality measures and stop rating individuals on it alone

explanation.correct: When a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure (Goodhart's law). With volume and tooling unchanged, a sixfold drop in MTTR (4 hours to 40 minutes) arriving together with more reopened incidents and closures without evidence points to rushed closures, not better work. The fix is a balanced set of measures: speed (MTTR, time to triage) alongside quality (sampled closure reviews, reopen rate, missed detections found later), used to improve the process rather than to rank people. In a bank this matters beyond the SOC: an incident closed too early may never be classified against the DORA major-incident criteria, so a reportable incident can be missed.

distractors.a: Real efficiency gains do not arrive with more reopened incidents and missing evidence; ignoring the quality signals rewards the behaviour that produced them.
distractors.b: Clock drift would distort durations, but it cannot explain reopened incidents or empty closure notes. Checking the data is fine, but it does not account for the pattern.
distractors.c: Experience does make analysts faster, but not sixfold in six months at the same volume, and it would lower the reopen rate, not triple it. Treating the two trends as unrelated misses the cause.

explanation.interview_angle: Tests whether you know that a single speed metric tied to individual goals gets gamed, and how to measure quality alongside it.

references.title: NIST SP 800-55 Vol. 1: Measurement Guide for Information Security

questions.question: A rule that detects the creation of new local administrator accounts is reported as having a 70 % false-positive rate. Reviewing the closed alerts, you find that almost all were real account creations made by the IT team under approved change tickets. What does this mean for the metric and for tuning?

options.text: The detection logic is wrong and must be rewritten, because most of what it produces turns out to be incorrect
The alerts are benign true positives, so the metric is mislabelled and tuning should use change-ticket context
The rule should be disabled, because a 70 % false-positive rate means it costs more than it finds
The logic is fine but needs a count threshold, so that only bursts of new admin accounts raise an alert

explanation.correct: A false positive means the rule fired on something it should not have matched (wrong logic or bad data). Here the rule matched real admin-account creations, which is its job; the activity was simply authorised. That is a benign true positive. Counting it as a false positive makes a working rule look broken and pushes people to weaken it. Microsoft Sentinel, for example, keeps them apart when an incident is closed: 'Benign Positive - suspicious but expected' versus 'False Positive - incorrect alert logic' or 'incorrect data'. The tuning that fits is contextual: suppress or downgrade creations that match an approved change (for example via a watchlist of approved changes or admins), so unapproved creations still alert.

distractors.a: Rewriting the logic would 'fix' something that is not broken: the rule correctly detected account creation.
distractors.c: Disabling it removes detection of unauthorised local admin accounts, a common persistence step (MITRE ATT&CK T1136.001), because of a labelling error.
distractors.d: A single unauthorised admin account is the event that matters; a count threshold would hide exactly the case the rule exists for.

explanation.interview_angle: Do you know the difference between a false positive and a benign true positive, and why mixing them corrupts tuning decisions?

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Navigate and triage incidents in Microsoft Sentinel
Microsoft Learn: Handle false positives in Microsoft Sentinel
MITRE ATT&CK T1136.001: Create Account: Local Account

questions.question: A security vendor's detection team is moving to detection-as-code. Which THREE practices belong to that approach? (Choose 3.)

options.text: Rules are stored as files in a version-control repository, so every change has an author, a diff and a history
Rule changes are proposed as pull requests and reviewed by a second engineer before they are merged
Rules are edited directly in the production SIEM console and exported to the repository once a quarter
A CI pipeline validates rule syntax and replays stored malicious and benign sample events before deployment
Only the current production version of each rule is kept, so that older versions cannot cause confusion

explanation.correct: Detection-as-code applies software engineering practice to detections: rules live as files in version control (who changed what, when and why, with the ability to revert), changes go through peer review in a pull request, and an automated pipeline checks syntax and replays known-bad and known-benign samples before anything reaches production. Microsoft Sentinel, for example, can deploy custom content such as analytics rules from a connected GitHub or Azure DevOps repository, and Sigma is an open, vendor-neutral rule format that is commonly kept in such repositories.

distractors.c: Console-first editing with a quarterly export turns the repository into a stale copy: production differs from what was reviewed, and the changes in between have no review or history.
distractors.e: Throwing away history removes the main benefit of version control: you can no longer see what changed before a regression or roll back to the last version that worked.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Deploy content as code from your repository (Microsoft Sentinel)
SigmaHQ: Sigma rule repository

questions.question: A vendor's detection pipeline is configured as in the fragment below. Last night a rule change that fails its sample-event tests was merged into main. What happened to that rule?
questions.context:
# .gitlab-ci.yml (fragment)
stages: [lint, test, deploy]

lint_rules:
  stage: lint
  script: ./tools/lint_rules.sh rules/

test_rules:
  stage: test
  script: python3 tools/replay_samples.py --rules rules/ --samples samples/
  allow_failure: true

deploy_prod:
  stage: deploy
  script: python3 tools/deploy.py --target production
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"

options.text: It was deployed to production: the failed test job only raised a warning and the pipeline went on to deploy
It was not deployed, because any failed job stops all jobs in the later stages of the pipeline
It was not deployed, because deploy_prod only runs in merge request pipelines and never for commits on main
It was deployed to a staging target only, because the test stage reported a failure

explanation.correct: In GitLab CI, allow_failure: true lets the pipeline continue with later jobs when that job fails; the job shows a warning and the pipeline still counts as successful. deploy_prod uses the default when: on_success and its rule matches pipelines on main, so the rule that failed its replay tests went to production. In detection-as-code the tests are the quality gate: a rule that no longer fires on its malicious sample, or fires on its benign one, must block deployment. Typical fixes: remove allow_failure from the test job, require a passing pipeline before merging to main, and keep allow_failure only for checks that are genuinely advisory.

distractors.b: That is GitLab's default behaviour, but allow_failure: true on test_rules overrides it for that job.
distractors.c: The rule checks $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main", which is true for the pipeline that runs when the merge commit lands on main.
distractors.d: Nothing in the configuration defines a staging target or a separate path on failure; the only deploy job targets production.

explanation.interview_angle: Can you read a pipeline and see where the quality gate leaks, instead of assuming that having CI means tests block bad rules?

references.title: GitLab Docs: CI/CD YAML syntax reference (allow_failure, when)

questions.question: True or false: when detection rules are deployed from a repository by a pipeline, a correct emergency fix typed directly into the SIEM console can be lost later even if nobody edits that rule by hand again.

options.text: True
False

explanation.correct: True. The repository still holds the old version, so the next deployment from it can silently overwrite the console fix and bring the problem back. Microsoft's guidance for Sentinel repository connections says exactly this: edit connected content in the repository, and if you edit it in Sentinel, export it back to source control or it can be overwritten at the next deployment. The console edit also skipped peer review and the test pipeline and left no history explaining it. Emergency changes are legitimate, but they should go through an expedited path in the same pipeline, or be committed back immediately with a reference to the incident.

distractors.b: Believing a correct change is automatically safe ignores configuration drift: production and repository now differ, and the pipeline treats the repository as the source of truth.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Deploy content as code from your repository (Microsoft Sentinel)

questions.question: Put the steps of a detection-as-code change in order, from the idea to feedback from production.

options.text: Open a pull request: the CI pipeline validates the rule and replays the samples, and a peer reviews the change
Monitor the rule's alert volume and precision in production and send tuning back as new changes
Define what to detect: the technique, the data source it needs, and confirm that data is actually collected
Merge into the main branch, which triggers the pipeline to deploy the rule
Write the rule and its malicious and benign test samples in a feature branch

explanation.correct: First define the goal (for example a MITRE ATT&CK technique), the log source it requires, and whether that data is really being ingested; without data the rule cannot work. Then write the rule together with its test samples in a branch. The pull request runs the automated checks and gets a human review. Merging to main deploys it through the pipeline, never by hand. Finally, watch how it behaves in production (volume, true versus false positive closures) and feed tuning back through the same loop. Frameworks such as Palantir's Alerting and Detection Strategy (ADS) formalise this by requiring sections such as blind spots, false positives and validation before a detection goes live.

references.title: Palantir: Alerting and Detection Strategy (ADS) Framework
Microsoft Learn: Deploy custom content from your repository (Microsoft Sentinel)

questions.question: An MSSP runs this function on every alert; a later automation step auto-closes alerts whose source IP has reputation "clean". Which statement about the function's behaviour is correct?

options.text: If the TI service does not answer within 5 seconds, the alert is enriched as "clean"
If the service answers HTTP 429 (rate limited), the alert is enriched as "clean" and can be auto-closed
If the JSON response has no "verdict" key, the function raises a KeyError and the alert stays unenriched
The IP address is sent in the request body, so it never appears in the URL that the TI provider receives

explanation.correct: Any non-200 status, including 429 when the MSSP exceeds its API quota and 5xx during a provider outage, returns reputation "clean". A failed lookup becomes indistinguishable from a real clean verdict, and the auto-close step then closes those alerts unseen, so the enrichment fails open exactly on busy days when quotas run out. Safer code returns an explicit state such as "lookup_failed" (or calls r.raise_for_status() and handles the error) and keeps those alerts in the queue.

distractors.a: On a timeout, requests raises a Timeout exception; nothing here catches it, so the function errors out instead of returning "clean". That is a robustness problem too, but a different one.
distractors.c: dict.get("verdict", "unknown") returns the default "unknown" when the key is missing; only square-bracket access such as alert["src_ip"] raises KeyError.
distractors.d: The IP is concatenated into the URL path (TI_URL + ip) of a GET request; there is no request body at all.

explanation.interview_angle: Can you spot a fail-open path in automation code, the kind of bug that silently closes real alerts?

references.title: Requests documentation: Quickstart (status codes, timeouts, exceptions)

questions.question: An L2 analyst runs this script at the start of each shift. What does its output show?
questions.context:
$since = (Get-Date).ToUniversalTime().AddHours(-24).ToString("o")
$uri   = "https://siem.example.com/api/v2/alerts?status=new&since=$since"
$resp  = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri $uri -Headers @{ Authorization = "Bearer $token" }
$resp.items |
  Where-Object { $_.severity -eq "high" } |
  Group-Object -Property rule_name |
  Sort-Object -Property Count -Descending |
  Select-Object -First 5 -Property Name, Count

options.text: The five most recent high-severity alerts of the last 24 hours, newest first
The five hosts with the most new high or critical alerts in the last 24 hours
The five rules with the most new alerts of exactly 'high' severity in the last 24 hours, with their counts
The five rules with the most high alerts since the SIEM was installed, because Invoke-RestMethod drops the 'since' value

explanation.correct: Read the pipeline step by step: the API call asks for new alerts from the last 24 hours; Where-Object keeps those whose severity equals 'high' (PowerShell's -eq is case-insensitive for strings, so 'High' matches too, but 'critical' does not); Group-Object groups them by rule_name and exposes Name and Count; Sort-Object orders the groups by Count, largest first; Select-Object keeps the top five. The output is the noisiest high-severity rules of the day, a quick view of what is driving the queue. One caveat: if the API paginates, reading only $resp.items from the first response can understate the counts.

distractors.a: Nothing sorts by time, and Group-Object collapses individual alerts into groups, so the output is per rule, not per alert.
distractors.b: The grouping key is rule_name, not a host field, and -eq "high" excludes 'critical' alerts.
distractors.d: The since value is part of the URL query string and is sent to the API like any other parameter; Invoke-RestMethod does not remove it.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Group-Object (PowerShell)
Microsoft Learn: about_Comparison_Operators (PowerShell)

questions.question: An MSSP engineer uses this script to extract the user and source IP from a client's VPN log before loading them into the SIEM. Which sample lines will be silently skipped?
questions.context:
import re
pat = re.compile(r"user=(\w+) src=(\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)")

with open("vpn.log") as f:
    for line in f:
        m = pat.search(line)
        if m:
            emit(user=m.group(1), src=m.group(2))

# sample lines from vpn.log
# 1: 2026-10-20T07:58:12Z login ok   user=apopescu src=198.51.100.23
# 2: 2026-10-20T08:01:40Z login ok   user=a.ionescu src=203.0.113.77
# 3: 2026-10-20T08:03:05Z login fail user=svc-backup src=198.51.100.4
# 4: 2026-10-20T08:04:51Z login ok   user=mdumitru src=203.0.113.9

options.text: Only line 3, because the pattern does not match failed logins
None of them, because search() looks for a match anywhere in the line
Only line 2, because the dot in the username acts as a regex wildcard and confuses the match
Lines 2 and 3, because \w does not match "." or "-", so those usernames break the pattern

explanation.correct: \w matches letters, digits and underscore only. For 'a.ionescu' and 'svc-backup' the engine matches 'a' or 'svc', then expects a space before 'src=' and finds '.' or '-', so the line has no match. The script simply ignores lines without a match, so those events never reach the SIEM and nothing reports the loss: dotted personal accounts and hyphenated service accounts, often the most interesting ones, become invisible to every rule. Robust parsers count or forward unparsed lines (a parse-failure metric or a raw fallback), and onboarding tests should include a sample line for every username format the client uses.

distractors.a: The pattern never looks at 'ok' or 'fail'; line 3 fails because of the hyphen in the username, not because the login failed.
distractors.b: search() tries every starting position, but the whole pattern must still match from there; each line has only one 'user=', so no other position can succeed.
distractors.c: A dot is special inside the pattern, not inside the text being searched. Line 2 fails because \w does not match '.', and line 3 fails as well because of the hyphen.

explanation.interview_angle: Shows whether you can read a short parser and predict silent data loss, a common onboarding failure.

references.title: Python documentation: re (regular expression operations)

questions.question: After a new firewall is onboarded, an analyst searching a 15-minute window around a confirmed malware download finds the proxy events but no firewall events. The firewall events for that connection do exist, but every one is stamped exactly three hours later than the matching proxy event. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The firewall writes local time without a timezone offset, and the SIEM parses it as UTC
The firewall events reach the SIEM with a three-hour ingestion delay and have not fully arrived
The firewall logged a different, later session, because it reset the original connection
The search window is too short, and it should be widened to four hours for firewall data

explanation.correct: A constant whole-hour offset between two sources describing the same connection is the signature of a timezone problem. Many appliances log local time with no offset; if the parser assumes UTC, a device in Romania on summer time (UTC+3) is stored three hours later than reality. Every time-bounded search, timeline and correlation rule then misses or misorders its events. The fix belongs to onboarding: make the device log in UTC or include the offset, or set the source's timezone in the parser (for example the TZ setting in Splunk's props.conf), then confirm by comparing event time with ingestion time; in Microsoft Sentinel, TimeGenerated against ingestion_time() exposes this kind of skew.

distractors.b: Ingestion delay changes when events arrive, not the time written inside them; these events are already searchable, just at the wrong time.
distractors.c: Different sessions would not line up with exactly the same three-hour offset on every connection; a fixed whole-hour shift points to time parsing, not to traffic.
distractors.d: Widening the window hides the defect and still breaks rules that depend on precise ordering; fix the timestamp, not the search.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: ingestion_time() function (KQL)
Microsoft Learn: Log data ingestion time in Azure Monitor
NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management

questions.question: An MSSP is onboarding a new client's domain controller logs. Which THREE checks should pass before the source is declared live for detection? (Choose 3.)

options.text: Key fields such as account name, logon type and source IP land in the normalised fields that the rules query, not only in the raw message
Event time is parsed correctly, and the gap between event time and ingestion time is known and small
The detection rules for the new source are switched to automatic containment, since the data is fresh
A health alert fires if the source stops sending or its volume drops far below its normal baseline
The audit policy on the domain controllers is left at default, since the SIEM infers missing event types by correlation

explanation.correct: A source only helps detection if the rules can read it, on time, all the time. Parsing: rules query normalised fields (for example ECS user.name in Elastic, the CIM user field in Splunk, TargetUserName in Microsoft Sentinel's SecurityEvent table); if parsing fails, every rule on that source silently returns nothing. Time: a wrong timezone or large ingestion delay breaks correlation windows. Health: a source that stops sending produces no alerts, which looks exactly like 'nothing happened'. Microsoft Sentinel offers data-connector health monitoring (the SentinelHealth table for supported connectors), and a 'no events for N minutes' rule works on any SIEM.

distractors.c: A new source needs a tuning period first; automatic containment on untuned rules risks disrupting the client's business on false positives.
distractors.e: A SIEM can only analyse what the source records. Default Windows audit policy does not log some events your rules need (process creation, 4688, is off by default), and correlation cannot recreate events that were never generated.

explanation.interview_angle: Tests whether you know that most 'missed detections' start as onboarding gaps: unparsed fields, bad timestamps and silent sources.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Monitor the health of your data connectors
Elastic Common Schema (ECS) reference

questions.question: Since a bank added a second log collector for high availability, a threshold rule ('more than 20 failed logons for one account in 10 minutes') has been firing for accounts that the help desk confirms failed only 11 or 12 times. Based on the search output below, what is the cause?
questions.context:
search: failed logons, account=t.marin, host=WS-0412, last 10 min
group by EventRecordID

EventRecordID  count  collectors
884213         2      col-01, col-02
884219         2      col-01, col-02
884226         2      col-01, col-02
...            ...    ...
(11 rows)      total events: 22

options.text: The account is the target of a password-spraying attack that the help desk could not see
Each failed logon is recorded once on the domain controller and once on the workstation, and the rule adds both
Both collectors forward the same events, so every failed logon is stored twice and the rule counts duplicates
Consecutive runs of the rule overlap in time, so each event is counted in two different executions

explanation.correct: Each EventRecordID, the Windows event log's own sequence number on that host, appears twice, once per collector. The same failed logon has been stored twice, so 11 real failures become 22 and cross the threshold of 20. Duplicates inflate every count-based rule and metric (failed logons, volumes, ingestion cost) and confuse investigations. Fix it in the pipeline: run the HA pair active/passive or load-balanced so each event is sent once, or deduplicate at ingestion on a stable key (host + channel + EventRecordID); counting distinct record IDs in the rule is only a temporary safety net.

distractors.a: A spraying attack produces many distinct events, each with its own record ID. Here 22 events are only 11 unique IDs, each stored twice, which matches what the help desk saw.
distractors.b: That double counting is real when a rule sums workstation and domain-controller logs: the workstation records 4625 while the DC records 4771 (Kerberos pre-authentication failed) or 4776 (NTLM credential validation failed), each with its own record ID on its own host. Here the search is already limited to host=WS-0412 and the same record ID arrives twice through two collectors, so the cause is the pipeline, not a second host.
distractors.d: Overlapping runs can make a rule fire twice on one burst, but they cannot make a single search over one window return each record twice; the duplication is in the stored data.

explanation.interview_angle: Can you use a unique event identifier to prove a data-pipeline defect instead of chasing a phantom attack?

references.title: NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management

questions.question: A bank's CFO asks the SOC to cut SIEM costs by about 30 %. Which proposal reduces cost while keeping the ability to detect and investigate?

options.text: Stop collecting identity-provider sign-in logs, because they are among the largest sources by event count and grow fastest
Cut retention for every source to 14 days, on the basis that most investigations start within two weeks of the first alert
Keep detection-critical sources in the full tier; move verbose firewall and flow logs to a cheaper, searchable tier
Ingest a 10 % random sample of every source, so each one stays represented at a fraction of the cost

explanation.correct: Not all data has the same detection value. Primary sources (identity sign-ins, EDR, cloud audit trails, alerts from other tools) feed real-time rules and belong in the full-featured, more expensive tier. High-volume secondary sources (firewall, proxy, NetFlow, storage access logs) are used mostly for context and investigation, so they can live in a cheaper tier that is searchable on demand. Microsoft Sentinel describes exactly this split between its analytics tier and data lake tier; in Splunk the equivalent decision is which index, and which retention, each source gets. Before moving anything, check which rules depend on it, and keep the retention that the bank's policy and regulators require.

distractors.a: Identity logs are among the highest-value sources: credential abuse and impossible-travel detections depend on them. Volume is the wrong criterion for cutting.
distractors.b: Intrusions are often discovered weeks or months after initial access, and banks have retention obligations; 14 days would leave investigations without history.
distractors.d: Random sampling breaks counting rules (failed-logon thresholds), sequence detections and forensic completeness: the one event that mattered has a 90 % chance of being dropped.

explanation.interview_angle: Shows whether you can defend a cost cut in terms of detection value instead of raw volume.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Log retention tiers in Microsoft Sentinel
Microsoft Learn: Reduce costs for Microsoft Sentinel
