SigninLogs            95
AuditLogs             12

options.text: Cutting SecurityEvent is the obvious first saving, because Windows security events are mostly routine logon noise
CommonSecurityLog drives most of the cost; break it down by device and activity and check rule dependencies first
CommonSecurityLog must hold mostly low-value data, because the largest table in a SIEM is usually the noisiest one
Only SigninLogs matters for detection, so every other table can move to the cheapest tier

explanation.correct: The output answers one question: where the volume, and therefore the cost, is. CommonSecurityLog (CEF-formatted logs from firewalls, proxies and similar appliances) is about 62 % of the roughly 6.7 TB. That makes it the first place to look, but it says nothing about detection value. The next step is to split it further, for example CommonSecurityLog | summarize count() by DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, Activity, to find verbose subsets such as allowed internal traffic, and then check which analytics rules, hunting queries and reports depend on them before filtering them or moving them to a cheaper tier. (In the Usage table, Quantity is in MB, hence the division by 1000.)

distractors.a: SecurityEvent carries logons, process creation and log clearing (4624, 4688, 1102); calling it noise without checking which rules use it risks removing core detections.
distractors.c: Volume and value are different axes; the same table can hold both noisy allow logs and the deny or threat events that rules rely on. This output cannot tell you which.
distractors.d: Sign-in logs are valuable but far from the only detection source; endpoint, firewall and audit data feed many rules. The output gives no basis for such a sweeping move.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Analyze usage in a Log Analytics workspace
Microsoft Learn: Reduce costs for Microsoft Sentinel

questions.question: You are moving between SIEM platforms. Match each platform term to the general concept it represents.

left.text: Splunk source type
Elastic Common Schema (ECS)
Microsoft Sentinel watchlist
QRadar offense

right.text: A shared field-naming standard used to normalise events from different sources
A record grouping related events that triggered correlation rules, investigated as one case
A label that tells the platform how to parse and interpret a particular data format
A reference list, such as high-value assets or leavers, joined into queries and rules
An agent installed on endpoints that forwards their logs to the SIEM

explanation.correct: A Splunk source type is assigned to incoming data and tells Splunk how to break, timestamp and extract fields for that format. ECS is an open specification of common field names (for example source.ip, user.name) so that data from different products can be queried the same way; Splunk's CIM and Microsoft Sentinel's ASIM play a similar role. A Sentinel watchlist is reference data (a lookup) that rules and hunts join against, comparable to a Splunk lookup or a QRadar reference set. A QRadar offense groups the events and flows behind fired rules into one item to investigate, similar in purpose to an incident in Sentinel. Knowing these equivalents lets you port skills and detections between platforms.

distractors.l1: The forwarding agent (r5) is a different component; a source type is the parsing label given to data once it arrives.
distractors.l3: A watchlist is not a schema (r1); it does not rename fields, it supplies values that queries match or enrich against.

explanation.interview_angle: Interviewers check that you understand concepts, not one vendor's menus, so you can switch platforms quickly.

references.title: Splunk Docs: Why source types matter
Elastic Common Schema (ECS) reference
Microsoft Learn: Watchlists in Microsoft Sentinel

questions.question: An MSSP serves clients on three different SIEM platforms and plans to write each detection once in Sigma, then convert it for every platform. What is the main limitation the team must plan for?

options.text: Each converted query depends on correct field and log-source mappings per client, so it still needs testing
A Sigma rule can be converted for only one SIEM platform, which has to be chosen when the rule is first written
Sigma can only express free-text keyword searches, not conditions on specific field values
Sigma rules run on a separate engine, so every client must forward a copy of all its logs to the MSSP for matching

explanation.correct: Sigma is a generic YAML rule format; backends (pySigma, used by sigma-cli) convert it into each platform's query language, and processing pipelines map Sigma's generic field names and log sources onto each environment's real fields and tables. That mapping is where conversions go wrong: a client whose proxy logs use different field names, or whose parser leaves a field empty, receives a syntactically valid query that never matches. The MSSP therefore still needs per-client mappings, conversion inside CI, and tests against each client's own sample events.

distractors.b: One Sigma rule can be converted to many targets; that portability is the point of the format.
distractors.c: Sigma's detection section is built on field-value selections with modifiers such as contains or endswith; keyword searches are only one option.
distractors.d: Converted Sigma rules become native queries that run inside each SIEM; no separate engine or copy of the logs is needed.

references.title: Sigma documentation: Backends and pipelines
Sigma documentation: Rules

questions.question: An internal auditor at a bank asks the SOC to prove that its detection for privileged-account misuse actually works. Which evidence answers the question best?

options.text: A screenshot showing that the rule is enabled in the SIEM, together with its last-modified date
A report showing that the rule produced no alerts at all last quarter, which means that no misuse took place
The vendor's statement that the content pack containing the rule is certified for the banking sector
A dated test record: a controlled simulation of the misuse, the alert it raised, and how it was handled

explanation.correct: 'Works' means detection end to end: the source logs the activity, the data reaches the SIEM and is parsed, the rule fires, and someone acts on the alert. Only a test exercises the whole chain. A good record names the use case and its owner, the technique simulated (for example adding an account to a privileged group, MITRE ATT&CK T1098 Account Manipulation), the date, the alert ID produced, the handling, and the follow-up if it failed. Frameworks such as Palantir's ADS make a validation section mandatory for this reason, and banks commonly retest critical use cases on a schedule and after major changes to the log source or the rule.

distractors.a: Enabled is not the same as working: a rule can be enabled while its log source has stopped sending or a field it relies on has been renamed.
distractors.b: Silence proves nothing by itself; a broken rule or a missing data source also produces zero alerts.
distractors.c: A vendor statement covers the content as shipped, not this bank's data sources, parsers and tuning.

explanation.interview_angle: Tests whether you know that detection assurance comes from testing, not from configuration screenshots or quiet dashboards.

references.title: Palantir: Alerting and Detection Strategy (ADS) Framework
MITRE ATT&CK T1098: Account Manipulation

questions.question: In an MSSP's shared queue, one client's misconfigured application starts generating about 5,000 alerts an hour from a single rule. Other clients' high-severity alerts are now drifting toward their SLA limits. What is the right immediate action?

options.text: Keep working the queue strictly first-in, first-out, so every client is treated the same way under contract
Disable the noisy rule across all clients until the one affected client has fixed its misconfigured application
Group that client's flood or suppress it for a set time, tell the client, and keep triaging others by priority
Bulk-delete the flood alerts, because the misconfiguration has clearly caused them and they add nothing of value

explanation.correct: A flood from one tenant must not consume the whole SOC. Grouping the alerts into one incident, or a suppression scoped to that rule and that client that expires automatically, protects other clients' SLAs while keeping the flood visible. The client must be told, because they own the fix and because a flood can hide real malicious activity in their environment. Someone should still sample the flood: 'misconfiguration' is a hypothesis until checked. Record the suppression and remove it once the source is fixed; in Microsoft Sentinel, for example, automation rules can be scoped and given an expiration.

distractors.a: FIFO lets one tenant's noise push other clients' high-severity alerts past their SLA; queues are worked by priority, not arrival order.
distractors.b: Disabling the rule for every tenant blinds clients that have no problem, to solve one client's issue.
distractors.d: Deleting alerts destroys evidence and the audit trail, and the flood may contain or hide malicious activity.

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Automate threat response with automation rules in Microsoft Sentinel
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

questions.question: To reduce alert fatigue, four rule exclusions have been proposed for review (below). Which TWO are acceptable as written? (Choose 2.)
questions.context:
EXC-1  rule: Encoded PowerShell
       exclude where process = "powershell.exe" and command_line contains "-EncodedCommand"
       owner: (none)   expires: never

EXC-2  rule: Encoded PowerShell
       exclude where parent_process = "C:\Program Files\DeployAgent\agent.exe"
                 and signer = "Example Corp" and host_group = "Workstations"
       owner: endpoint-team   ticket: CHG-4471   review: 2027-01-31

EXC-3  rule: Mass file read on file servers
       exclude where user = "svc_backup"
       owner: (none)   expires: never

EXC-4  rule: Internal port scan
       exclude where src_ip = "10.20.5.15" (vulnerability scanner)
                 and time between Sat 01:00-04:00
       owner: vuln-mgmt   ticket: CHG-4502   review: 2027-01-31

options.text: EXC-1
EXC-2
EXC-3
EXC-4

explanation.correct: A safe exclusion is as narrow as the benign activity, and it is owned, justified and reviewed. EXC-2 combines parent process path, code signer and host group, so only the deployment agent's own PowerShell is skipped, and it has an owner, a change ticket and a review date. EXC-4 limits the scanner's address to its documented scan window on the one rule it trips, again with an owner and a review date. Both leave the rule working for everything else. Microsoft Sentinel's guidance, for example, prefers exceptions kept in a watchlist referenced by the rule, or automation-rule exceptions that expire, so that exceptions stay visible and time-bound.

distractors.a: EXC-1 excludes exactly what the rule detects (powershell.exe with -EncodedCommand), so the rule can never fire again: a disabled rule disguised as tuning, with no owner or expiry.
distractors.c: EXC-3 removes the backup account from the rule on every server, forever. Accounts with broad read access are exactly what attackers reuse for collection and exfiltration; an acceptable version would also pin the backup host, process and window, with an owner and review date.

explanation.interview_angle: Can you tell a scoped, governed exception from one that quietly turns a rule off?

references.title: Microsoft Learn: Handle false positives in Microsoft Sentinel

questions.question: The CISO of a bank needs one page from the SOC for the board's risk committee each quarter. Which content fits that audience?

options.text: Alert totals, events per second and active-rule counts, each with quarter-on-quarter trend charts
Material incidents and impact, monitoring gaps on critical services with fix dates, regulatory reporting status
Every rule tuned this quarter with its false-positive rate, so the committee can see how much tuning effort went in
Ticket counts and average handling time per analyst, to demonstrate the team's productivity and its heavy workload

explanation.correct: A risk committee decides on risk acceptance and investment, so it needs risk-oriented information: incidents that mattered and what they cost or threatened, where critical business services (for example payments) are not adequately monitored and when that will be fixed, how key risk indicators moved against the agreed appetite, and whether any incident was, or should have been, reported to the regulator (under DORA, a major ICT-related incident triggers initial, intermediate and final reports). Alert volumes, EPS and per-rule false-positive rates belong in the SOC's internal reporting; they do not tell the board whether the bank's risk is rising or falling.

distractors.a: Volume metrics describe workload, not risk: more alerts can mean more attacks or simply worse tuning, and the board cannot act on either.
distractors.c: Rule-level tuning detail is useful to the SOC manager but far too granular for a risk committee, and it says nothing about business impact.
distractors.d: Per-analyst productivity is a line-management topic; it says nothing about the bank's exposure and, pushed up the chain, encourages speed over quality.

explanation.interview_angle: Can you translate SOC activity into the risk language a board uses?

references.title: NIST SP 800-55 Vol. 1: Measurement Guide for Information Security
Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 (DORA), Official Journal text

questions.question: The organisation starts using a SaaS file-sharing service. The vendor runs all the infrastructure, offers no syslog output and no way to install software on its servers, but publishes a REST audit-log API. The investigation team wants the service's audit trail in the SIEM. Which collection approach fits?

options.text: Ask the vendor to install the SIEM collection agent on the servers that host your tenant
Forward the laptops' Windows Security logs, which record the users' file-sharing actions
Poll the vendor's audit API with a connector that uses a dedicated read-only credential
Capture the TLS traffic to the service at the internet gateway and parse it into audit events

explanation.correct: SaaS audit trails are collected through the provider's API: a connector authenticates with a least-privilege (read-only) credential and polls the API or receives its notifications. In Microsoft Sentinel this is an API-based data connector; Microsoft 365 itself publishes its audit content through the Office 365 Management Activity API. That API's documentation shows two risks that apply to any API collection. First, events arrive in batches and not necessarily in the order they occurred. Second, content from a period when the subscription was stopped cannot be retrieved later. So an expired credential or a stopped subscription silently opens a gap, and the connector needs its own health monitoring.

distractors.a: In SaaS the provider operates the servers and customers do not get to install agents there; agent-based collection applies to systems you run yourself.
distractors.b: Windows Security logs record logons and local activity on the laptop, not the shares, downloads and permission changes that the SaaS service performs on its side.
distractors.d: Without TLS decryption the gateway sees only the destination and byte counts. Even with decryption, web traffic is not the service's authoritative record of shares and permission changes.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know that SaaS visibility depends on the provider's API, and that API collection brings its own latency and silent-failure risks.

references.title: Microsoft Sentinel data connectors
Office 365 Management Activity API reference

questions.question: An MSSP has just onboarded a client's new web proxy. An L1 analyst searching by source IP gets no proxy results, although the proxy events are in the SIEM: each one is stored as a single raw text line with the client IP, URL and action inside it, and no other fields are populated. Which pipeline stage is not working for this source?

options.text: Collection: the proxy is not sending its events to the collector
Parsing: the raw text is not being split into fields like client IP and URL
Normalisation: vendor field names are not yet mapped to the common schema names
Correlation: no rule joins the proxy events with events from other sources

explanation.correct: The events arrive, so collection works, but nothing has been extracted from the raw text, so there is no source-IP field to search. Parsing is the step that turns the raw line into fields (client IP, URL, action, user). Normalisation comes after it and renames those vendor fields to the common schema, for example SrcIpAddr in Microsoft Sentinel ASIM, src in the Splunk CIM or source.ip in Elastic ECS. Typical causes are a missing or wrong parser (or sourcetype) or a log format the parser does not expect. Until it is fixed, analysts can only free-text search the raw message, which is slow and misses values written differently.

distractors.a: Collection is working: the events are in the SIEM, just unstructured.
distractors.c: Normalisation renames fields a parser has already extracted; here no fields exist yet, so there is nothing to map.
distractors.d: Correlation needs parsed fields to join on; a missing rule would not explain why a simple search by source IP returns nothing.

references.title: NIST SP 800-92, Guide to Computer Security Log Management (log parsing and normalization)
Normalization and the Advanced Security Information Model (ASIM)

questions.subtopic: Log sources for exfiltration: email gateway
questions.question: A DLP alert says a user sent a spreadsheet with customer data to a personal webmail address. Before escalating, the L1 analyst must confirm whether the message actually left the organisation or was held back. Which log source answers that directly?

options.text: Web proxy logs for the user's workstation
Identity provider sign-in logs for the user
Endpoint process logs showing the mail client running
Email gateway or message trace logs for that message

explanation.correct: The email gateway, or the mail platform's message trace, records each message's sender, recipients and attachments together with its final status: delivered, failed, pending, quarantined or filtered. That status tells you whether data actually left. In Exchange Online, message trace shows whether the service received, rejected, deferred or delivered a message; on-premises, the secure email gateway's message log does the same job. A DLP policy can alert on the attempt even when the message is later blocked or quarantined, so check the delivery outcome before you judge severity.

distractors.a: Mail sent from the corporate mail client leaves through the mail servers over SMTP, not through the user's web proxy; the proxy would only help if the user had used a webmail site in the browser.
distractors.b: Sign-in logs show that the user authenticated, not what happened to a particular message.
distractors.c: Process telemetry shows the mail client was running, not whether the message was delivered.

references.title: Message trace in the Exchange admin center

questions.question: A client's rule should fire when a VPN session starts within 2 minutes after a burst of failed logons for the same account on the domain controllers (the VPN authenticates against them). During a purple-team test the rule stayed silent. Both event sets are in the SIEM with correctly populated user fields, and the failures exceed the rule's threshold. The analyst notices that the VPN appliance's clock runs 7 minutes behind the domain controllers. What is the most likely reason the rule missed?

options.text: VPN events are stamped 7 minutes early, so the session appears to precede the failures
The failed-logon threshold is too high for a short purple-team test and should be lowered for testing
The VPN appliance sends syslog over UDP, so the session-start event was lost in transit
The domain controller events were not normalised to the same schema as the VPN events

explanation.correct: Correlation windows compare timestamps written by different devices, so they only work if the clocks agree. The session really started about a minute after the failures, but the VPN appliance stamped it 7 minutes early, so in the SIEM it appears about 6 minutes before the failures and 'session after failures within 2 minutes' never holds. NIST SP 800-92 gives exactly this example: an inaccurate host clock can make event A look as if it happened before event B when it happened after. Fix it at the source: sync every device to the organisation's designated time servers and alert on clock drift. Widening the window only hides the problem.

distractors.b: The stem says the failures already exceed the threshold; the problem is the order of events in time, not their number.
distractors.c: The session-start event is in the SIEM, so it was not lost. UDP loss is a real risk, but not the cause here.
distractors.d: The user fields are already populated and joinable; the rule fails on its time condition, not on field names.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you treat clock drift as a detection failure, not just a cosmetic timeline problem.

references.title: NIST SP 800-92, Guide to Computer Security Log Management (inconsistent timestamps)
ASD/CISA, Best practices for event logging and threat detection (timestamp consistency)

questions.question: A bank employee who resigned last week is suspected of taking client files from the corporate cloud file storage. The analyst's SIEM query on the cloud audit log, filtered on the operation that records browser downloads, returns 12 files. The endpoint team reports about 3,000 client files in the sync folder on the user's laptop, created in the last few days. What is the most likely explanation for the difference?

options.text: Cloud audit events take several days to reach the SIEM, so most of the downloads have not arrived yet
The 3,000 files were probably copied in from a USB drive, since every cloud download would appear in the query
The files were pulled by the desktop sync client, which the audit log records under a different operation
The endpoint creation times are unreliable, so the files most likely predate the resignation and can be ignored

explanation.correct: Cloud storage platforms log different download paths as different operations. In Microsoft 365, FileDownloaded is a download through the browser, while FileSyncDownloadedFull is a file downloaded to the computer by the OneDrive sync app; a mass-download search on FileDownloaded alone misses the sync path. 3,000 recently created files in the sync folder fit sync-client downloads, so rerun the query with every download-type operation (browser, sync client, and app or API access if relevant) before you size the incident. Before concluding anything from an audit log, check which operations record the activity you are looking for.

distractors.a: Audit ingestion delays are normally far shorter than a week, and you can measure them by comparing event time with ingestion time. A delay would also not explain why only one operation type appears.
distractors.b: This starts from the assumption that the query is complete, but it covered only one operation. USB is a hypothesis to test with endpoint evidence, not a conclusion to draw from an incomplete query.
distractors.d: Dismissing endpoint evidence because it does not fit the SIEM result is backwards. A sync client writes the local files when it downloads them, which matches cloud-side activity you have not queried yet.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you check that your query covers every way an activity can be logged before you put a number in the incident report.

references.title: Microsoft Purview: audit log activities (FileDownloaded, FileSyncDownloadedFull)
MITRE ATT&CK T1530 Data from Cloud Storage

questions.subtopic: Retention and storage tiers: PCI DSS
questions.question: A bank's SIEM team is redesigning storage for logs from its card-data environment, which falls under PCI DSS. Which design meets the standard's audit-log retention requirement at the lowest storage cost?

options.text: 30 days searchable in the SIEM, then 11 months in an archive that takes two days to restore
3 months searchable in the SIEM, then 9 more months in a cheaper archive tier
12 months in an archive tier only, restored on request for each investigation
3 months searchable in the SIEM, then deletion to limit the personal data kept
12 months fully searchable in the SIEM's most expensive analytics tier

explanation.correct: PCI DSS requirement 10.5.1: retain audit log history for at least 12 months, with at least the most recent three months immediately available for analysis. Design b is the cheapest one that meets both parts: three months in the searchable (hot) tier and the rest of the 12 months in cheaper storage. 'Immediately available' means you can query it now; data that needs a two-day restore does not count. Keeping all 12 months hot also complies, but costs more than the requirement needs. Other drivers, such as internal investigations, regulator requests or legal holds, may justify keeping data longer; record that as a documented decision.

distractors.a: Only 30 days are immediately available; the requirement needs the most recent three months searchable without a restore.
distractors.c: Archive-only storage fails the 'immediately available' part for the most recent three months.
distractors.d: Three months is the immediately available part, not the total; the history must cover at least 12 months.
distractors.e: Compliant, but keeping a full year in the most expensive tier goes beyond what 10.5.1 requires, and cost was part of the question.

references.title: Microsoft Entra ID and PCI-DSS Requirement 10 (quotes requirement 10.5.1)
ASD/CISA, Best practices for event logging and threat detection (hot and cold storage)

questions.question: To cut ingestion cost, a detection engineering team can move some log types to a cheaper tier that keeps data searchable for investigations but cannot be used by scheduled detection rules. Which log type is the best candidate to move?

options.text: Identity provider sign-in logs, which feed impossible-travel and password-spray rules
DLP policy-match events, which create the triage queue for the data-protection team
EDR alerts, which are correlated with identity events to raise incidents
Verbose firewall 'allow' flow records, mostly used for look-back in investigations

explanation.correct: The tier follows how the data is used. A source that feeds real-time or scheduled detections must stay in the tier the rules can query; a high-volume source that is mostly searched after the fact can move to the cheaper tier. Firewall allow/flow records are large, rarely alert on their own, and are valuable mainly for scoping ('where else did this IP connect?'). In Microsoft Sentinel / Azure Monitor this is the choice between the Analytics plan and the cheaper Basic or Auxiliary/Lake plans; Microsoft's documentation warns that alerts stop working for a table moved from Analytics to Auxiliary/Lake. Before moving anything, check that no active rule depends on the table, or the move silently breaks detection.

distractors.a: Sign-in logs feed core identity detections; moving them would silence those rules.
distractors.b: DLP matches are the data-protection team's alert stream and are low volume; moving them saves little and breaks triage.
distractors.c: EDR alerts are low volume and used in correlation rules, so they must stay where rules can query them.

references.title: Azure Monitor: configure a table plan (Analytics, Basic, Auxiliary/Lake)

questions.subtopic: Proxy log visibility and TLS inspection
questions.question: A bank's data-leakage team wants to investigate uploads to personal cloud storage using the web proxy logs already in the SIEM. For those sites, the proxy events show only the destination host on port 443, the user, and bytes sent and received: no URL path, no file name, no content inspection result. What explains this, and what would change it?

options.text: Logs reach the SIEM over plain UDP syslog, which drops fields; syslog over TLS would restore them
DNS query logs are not onboarded yet; adding them would supply the URL paths and uploaded file names
The proxy is not decrypting that HTTPS traffic; TLS inspection within privacy limits would expose it
Retention is too short and fields are trimmed as logs age; longer retention would keep the paths and file names

explanation.correct: Without TLS decryption a proxy sees the tunnel's destination (the CONNECT host or the SNI) and byte counts, not what is inside the HTTPS session, so it cannot log the URL path or file name or run DLP on the upload. TLS inspection decrypts at the proxy so full-URL filtering, file scanning and DLP can apply; Microsoft's documentation for Entra Internet Access, for example, describes TLS inspection as giving visibility into encrypted traffic for malware detection and data loss prevention. Expect gaps even after enabling it: privacy-sensitive categories are commonly excluded (Microsoft Entra Internet Access, for example, auto-creates an editable recommended bypass rule for the Education, Finance, Government and Health & Medicine categories, and tells you to communicate the TLS policy to users first), and applications that pin certificates must be bypassed or they fail the handshake. Until then, bytes sent per user per destination is still a useful volume signal.

distractors.a: Syslog over TLS protects the log stream between the proxy and the SIEM; it cannot add data the proxy never saw. The fields are missing at the source.
distractors.b: DNS logs show which domain was resolved, not the URL path or the uploaded file, and add little beyond the destination host the proxy already records.
distractors.d: Retention does not change what a single event contains; these fields were never captured.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can tell encrypting the log stream apart from decrypting the user's traffic, a common confusion.

references.title: Microsoft Entra Internet Access: what is TLS inspection?
Microsoft Entra Internet Access: configure TLS inspection policies (recommended bypass rule)
MITRE ATT&CK T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage

questions.question: An MSSP is onboarding a client's network devices, which can send syslog over UDP or over TLS. Which TWO are real limitations of plain UDP syslog that should be raised in the design review? (Choose 2)

options.text: UDP syslog requires installing an agent on every network device that sends logs
Lost messages are not detected or resent, so gaps can open without anyone being notified
UDP syslog can carry Linux system events only, so firewall or switch logs need another transport
Messages are sent in clear text with no sender authentication, so they can be read or forged
UDP syslog converts every timestamp to UTC on the way, which hides the device's original local time

explanation.correct: RFC 5426 (syslog over UDP) states that the transport has no mechanism to detect or correct lost datagrams, so messages can be lost without notice. It also provides no confidentiality and no strong sender authentication, so messages can be observed, forged or replayed on the path. Syslog over TLS (RFC 5425) runs over TCP and adds encryption and certificate-based authentication. Use TLS, or at least TCP, across untrusted network segments, and monitor each source for unexpected drops in volume whichever transport you choose.

distractors.a: Syslog is the agentless option: the device's built-in syslog function sends to a collector or forwarder (which may itself run an agent). Agents are needed for sources such as Windows event logs.
distractors.c: Firewalls, switches and proxies are among the most common syslog senders; the transport does not care what the message contains.
distractors.e: Syslog does not convert timestamps. Legacy BSD-format headers carry local time with no year and no time zone, which is the opposite problem.

references.title: RFC 5426, Transmission of Syslog Messages over UDP
RFC 5425, TLS Transport Mapping for Syslog

questions.question: After a client's firewall firmware upgrade, the firewall's event volume in the SIEM is unchanged, but a rule keyed on destination port has not fired for nine days, and the port field is empty in every event since the upgrade. The MSSP's health check, which alerts when a source goes silent, raised nothing. What is the most likely cause, and which control would have caught it?

options.text: A changed log format broke the parser's port extraction; monitor field fill rates, not only volume
The firewall stopped logging blocked connections; enable deny logging again and keep the silence check as it is
The rule's threshold is too strict for traffic after the upgrade; lower it until the rule starts firing again
Ingestion delay grew after the upgrade; lengthen the rule's look-back window so it covers the extra delay

explanation.correct: Unchanged volume plus a field that went empty at the moment of an upgrade points to parsing, not collection. The events still arrive, but the parser's pattern no longer matches the new layout, so dependent fields stay empty (or the whole event lands as raw text) and every rule on those fields goes blind without a single error. A volume or 'source silent' check cannot see this. Add data-quality checks per source: the share of events with key fields populated, parse-failure counts, and a test event replayed through critical detections after changes. Re-validate parsers after every vendor upgrade; joint ASD/CISA logging guidance recommends automated normalisation precisely because software and SaaS log formats can change over time or without notice.

distractors.b: Turning deny logging off would lower the event volume; it would not empty the port field in the events that still arrive.
distractors.c: The field the rule needs is empty; a lower threshold cannot make a rule match a value that is not there, and it would add noise once the parser is fixed.
distractors.d: A delay holds events back; it does not empty a field in events that are already in the SIEM.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you monitor log quality (are the fields there?) and not only log quantity.

references.title: ASD/CISA, Best practices for event logging and threat detection (content and format consistency)

questions.question: You are linking a DLP alert to proxy and EDR activity for the same person. The DLP tool records the user as j.doe@example.com, the proxy as EXAMPLE\jdoe, and the EDR mostly by the account's Windows SID. A colleague suggests joining the three sources on the laptop's IP address instead. What is the more reliable approach?

options.text: Join on the IP address, since every source logs it and in the same format
Resolve each identifier to one account through the directory and join on that key
Lowercase all the username fields in the SIEM so the three formats match
Treat any proxy or EDR event within a minute of the DLP alert as belonging to the user

explanation.correct: Different sources name the same account differently: user principal name, DOMAIN\sAMAccountName, SID. The directory (Active Directory / Entra ID) holds all of them for each account, so resolving every identifier to one canonical key gives a join that does not depend on network conditions. Common schemas plan for this: Microsoft Sentinel ASIM stores a username with its type (SrcUsername with SrcUsernameType such as UPN or Windows) and the user ID separately (SrcUserId with SrcUserIdType such as SID), and identity enrichment or a lookup table built from the directory maps between them. IP-based joins break with DHCP lease changes, VPN address pools, NAT and shared or multi-user hosts, so use the IP only as supporting evidence within a short, verified time range.

distractors.a: IP addresses change with DHCP, VPN and NAT, and several users can share one; an IP join can attach the alert to the wrong person.
distractors.c: Case is not the problem: a UPN, a DOMAIN\name and a SID are different identifiers, and no text clean-up turns a SID into a UPN.
distractors.d: Time alone links whatever happened nearby, including other users' activity on shared systems; that is not attribution.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can explain why entity resolution, not a convenient common field, is the basis of cross-source correlation.

references.title: ASIM user entity (username and user ID types)

questions.question: Which of these detections can only be built as a correlation across two log sources, rather than as a rule on a single event?

options.text: A server's Security event log being cleared, recorded as Windows event 1102
A DLP policy match on an outbound document that contains several payment card numbers
A web proxy blocking a request to a URL categorised as malware distribution
A new-country sign-in followed within 30 minutes by a mass download from cloud storage

explanation.correct: The sign-in is recorded by the identity provider and the download by the cloud storage audit log. Only a rule that joins the two on the same user within a time window can express 'new-country sign-in, then mass download', a common pattern when a compromised account is used to take data. The other three are single events that are meaningful by themselves: one record from one source is enough to alert. Correlation rules depend on pipeline basics: both sources onboarded, the user identifier normalised to the same form, and clocks in sync.

distractors.a: Event 1102 is a strong signal on its own; no second source is needed to alert on it.
distractors.b: The DLP engine has already done the content analysis; the match is one event from one source.
distractors.c: The category and the block decision are both in a single proxy log line.

references.title: NIST SP 800-92, Guide to Computer Security Log Management (event correlation)
MITRE ATT&CK T1530 Data from Cloud Storage

questions.question: An IR lead at a bank is writing the incident timeline that will support the report to the regulator. Some events reached the SIEM hours late because a cloud API connector was backlogged. Which timestamp should the timeline be built on?

options.text: When each event occurred at its source, in UTC, with ingestion time kept as a separate field
The SIEM ingestion time of each event, since it comes from one clock for every source
The time the first alert reached an analyst, since that is when the bank became aware
The local time each source displays, left unconverted so that it matches the original evidence

explanation.correct: A timeline describes what happened when, so it uses event time: when the action occurred at the source (usually TimeGenerated in Microsoft Sentinel, _time in Splunk, @timestamp in Elastic ECS), normalised to one zone, normally UTC. Ingestion time (ingestion_time() in KQL, _indextime in Splunk, event.ingested in ECS) records when the SIEM received the event. Keep it, because it explains why an alert fired late, but ordering by it would put backlogged events hours after the actions they record. The 'became aware' moment is a separate milestone in the report: it starts regulatory clocks such as GDPR's 72 hours and DORA's 24-hour limit for the initial notification, but it is not the time of each action.

distractors.b: Ingestion time is uniform but it measures the pipeline, not the incident: delayed events would appear hours after they happened and the sequence would be wrong.
distractors.c: Awareness time is one milestone in the report, not the time at which each action took place.
distractors.d: Mixing local times from sources in different zones, or across a daylight-saving change, misorders events. Keep the original value as evidence, but order on UTC.

references.title: Elastic Common Schema: event fields (@timestamp, event.created, event.ingested)
OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet (event time vs time of logging)

questions.question: A scheduled rule runs every 5 minutes and looks back 5 minutes on event time. Its source is a cloud audit feed whose events usually reach the SIEM 15 to 40 minutes after they occur. Tests show the rule almost never fires, although matching events are in the SIEM. What is the right fix?

options.text: Run the rule every minute instead of every 5 minutes, keeping the same look-back
Look back 24 hours on event time only and accept that the rule repeats its alerts on every run
Widen the event-time look-back by the delay and filter ingestion time to the last 5 minutes
Move the feed to a cheaper storage tier so that its events are ingested and searchable faster

explanation.correct: When the rule runs, a delayed event is not in the SIEM yet; by the next run its event time is already older than the 5-minute look-back, so no run ever sees it. The documented fix for Microsoft Sentinel scheduled rules: measure the delay (ingestion_time() minus TimeGenerated), widen the event-time look-back by that delay, and add an ingestion-time filter equal to the run interval so that overlapping windows do not alert twice on the same event. For example: OfficeActivity | where TimeGenerated >= ago(45m) | where ingestion_time() > ago(5m). In Splunk the same idea uses the _index_earliest / _index_latest modifiers alongside the event-time range. Near-real-time rules are another option where the platform supports them.

distractors.a: Running more often with the same 5-minute look-back still misses events that arrive 15 or more minutes late; frequency does not fix the window.
distractors.b: A 24-hour look-back on event time catches the events, but re-alerts on each one every 5 minutes for a day. Without the ingestion-time filter that is an alert flood.
distractors.d: The storage tier does not speed up delivery; the delay is upstream at the source, and cheaper tiers may not support scheduled rules at all.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know the difference between when an event happened and when your rule can see it.

references.title: Handle ingestion delay in scheduled analytics rules (Microsoft Sentinel)
Log data ingestion time in Azure Monitor

questions.question: An IR lead at a bank is scoping a suspected leak by a trader. The SIEM has: an on-premises web proxy (it only sees traffic from the office network), the email gateway, the cloud file storage audit log, and identity sign-in logs. There is no endpoint telemetry, and laptops reach the internet directly when used from home. Which TWO exfiltration paths would leave no trace in these sources? (Choose 2)

options.text: Copying files to a USB drive on the office laptop
Emailing files from the corporate mailbox to a personal address
Uploading files to personal cloud storage from the corporate laptop at home
Creating an 'anyone with the link' share on a corporate cloud storage folder
Uploading files to a personal webmail account from an office workstation

explanation.correct: Map each exfiltration channel to the sources that can see it. USB copies happen only on the endpoint; without EDR or endpoint DLP nothing in the SIEM records them (forensic artefacts such as USB device history may still exist on the laptop). Uploads from home bypass an on-premises proxy, so they are invisible unless traffic is forced through a cloud proxy or a full VPN tunnel. Corporate email passes the email gateway, sharing links are written to the cloud storage audit log, and webmail uploads from the office pass the proxy. Write the blind spots into the scoping notes: 'no record in the SIEM' must not be reported as 'did not happen'.

distractors.b: The email gateway records the outbound message, its recipients and its attachments.
distractors.d: Creating a sharing link is an operation in the cloud storage audit log (in Microsoft 365, AnonymousLinkCreated for an 'Anyone' link).
distractors.e: From the office network the upload passes the on-premises proxy, which logs at least the destination, the user and the bytes sent.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you state what your evidence cannot show before drawing conclusions from it.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1052.001 Exfiltration over USB
MITRE ATT&CK T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage

questions.question: The bank's data protection officer challenges the SIEM practice of keeping web proxy logs, with full URLs and usernames, indefinitely. Which response is the most defensible for the security team?

options.text: Banks are legally required to monitor security, so indefinite retention of all logs needs no further justification
Delete proxy logs after seven days, which removes the privacy concern while keeping the most recent activity
Anonymise usernames in all proxy logs at ingestion, so that the retention period no longer matters for privacy
Document a retention period per log type, justified by investigation and legal needs, then delete or aggregate

explanation.correct: GDPR's storage-limitation principle (art. 5(1)(e)) means personal data is kept no longer than necessary for its purpose, so 'forever, just in case' is hard to defend. Security monitoring is a legitimate purpose, but the period has to be justified. Joint ASD/CISA logging guidance says retention should follow a risk assessment and applicable regulatory requirements, and warns that incidents can take many months to discover; for card-data systems PCI DSS requires at least 12 months. Write the result into the retention policy per log type, limit who can query personal fields, and enforce deletion or aggregation automatically when the period ends.

distractors.a: A duty to monitor justifies keeping logs for a defined purpose and period; it does not switch off storage limitation or the need to document why.
distractors.b: Seven days is far shorter than many intrusions take to discover and below requirements such as PCI DSS 10.5.1, so investigations would lose their evidence.
distractors.c: Anonymising at ingestion makes it impossible to attribute activity to a person in an investigation. Pseudonymisation with controlled re-identification is a different and more workable option.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can balance security needs against data-protection law instead of treating one as overriding the other.

references.title: Art. 5 GDPR: Principles relating to processing of personal data (storage limitation, art. 5(1)(e))
ASD/CISA, Best practices for event logging and threat detection (event log retention)

questions.question: A bank's CISO asks for one metric in the management report that shows whether the SIEM can actually detect data exfiltration. Which metric answers that question?

options.text: Gigabytes of log data ingested per day, trended across the quarter for all sources
Share of exfiltration channels with a healthy log source and a tested detection
Number of detection rules currently enabled in the SIEM, compared with last quarter
Number of alerts the SOC closed each month, split by true and false positive

explanation.correct: Management needs to know where the bank is blind. Coverage per exfiltration channel (email, web upload, cloud storage sharing, removable media, print) shows for each one whether a log source feeds the SIEM and is healthy, and whether a detection has been tested against it; the uncovered channels go into the risk register. Volume, rule count and alert count measure activity: a SIEM can ingest terabytes and run hundreds of rules while never seeing USB copies or uploads from laptops off the corporate network. MITRE ATT&CK data components (the telemetry listed under each technique's detection section; the older data-source objects were deprecated in ATT&CK v18) help map which logs each exfiltration technique needs.

distractors.a: Ingested volume shows cost and load; a large volume can still leave entire channels unmonitored.
distractors.c: Rule count says nothing about whether the rules have the data they need or work; rules on missing or unparsed fields never fire.
distractors.d: Closed alerts measure workload and, split by outcome, tuning quality; they cannot show which exfiltration paths produce no alerts at all.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK data components
MITRE ATT&CK, Exfiltration (Tactic TA0010)

questions.subtopic: Timestamps and time zones in parsing
questions.question: An MSSP has onboarded a client's Linux web server. Its events appear in the SIEM with an event time later than the time the SIEM received them. Based on the evidence, what is the cause?
questions.context:
Raw message received by the collector:
<38>Mar 14 09:12:44 web01 sshd[2211]: Accepted publickey for deploy from 198.51.100.23 port 51122 ssh2

SIEM record:
EventTime=2026-03-14T09:12:44Z  ReceivedTime=2026-03-14T07:12:47Z  Host=web01

Other sources through the same collector: EventTime and ReceivedTime differ by less than 5 s.

On web01 (timedatectl):
Local time: Sat 2026-03-14 09:13:01 EET
Universal time: Sat 2026-03-14 07:13:01 UTC
Time zone: Europe/Bucharest (EET, +0200)
System clock synchronized: yes

options.text: The parser read the header's local time, which has no zone, as UTC
web01's clock is not synchronised and runs two hours ahead of real time
The collector's clock is two hours slow, so the received time is wrong
The events were held up in transit for about two hours before delivery

explanation.correct: The header is BSD-style syslog (RFC 3164): 'Mmm dd hh:mm:ss' in the sender's local time, with no year and no time zone. web01 runs on Europe/Bucharest time (EET, UTC+2) and its clock is synchronised, so 09:12:44 local is 07:12:44 UTC, which matches the received time. The parser stamped it as 09:12:44Z, which puts every event from this host two hours in the future, and the offset will change again when summer time starts. Fix it at the source or in the pipeline: send RFC 5424 syslog, whose timestamps carry a UTC offset, or set the source's time zone in the parser (TZ in Splunk props.conf; Elastic ECS has event.timezone for exactly this case). Then check other hosts onboarded with the same parser.

distractors.b: timedatectl shows the clock is synchronised and the UTC time is correct; the host's local time is simply UTC+2.
distractors.c: Other sources through the same collector show normal received times, so the collector clock is fine.
distractors.d: A transit delay makes the received time later than the event time; here it is the other way round, which no delay can produce.

references.title: RFC 3164, The BSD syslog Protocol (TIMESTAMP field)
Elastic Common Schema: event fields (event.timezone)

questions.question: An endpoint DLP alert at a bank reports a 2.1 GB upload to a personal cloud storage site at 23:40 UTC. The analyst queries the web proxy logs for the user and finds nothing between 23:00 and 01:00. Given the evidence, what should the analyst conclude?
questions.context:
Endpoint DLP alert 2026-05-04 23:40:12 UTC
User: EXAMPLE\m.trader07  Device: LT-0419  Action: allowed (audit only)
Activity: upload to cloud service via browser  Size: 2.1 GB

SIEM: proxy events per hour, all users (UTC)
2026-05-04 21:00   6,210
2026-05-04 22:00   5,995
2026-05-04 23:00       0
2026-05-05 00:00       0
2026-05-05 01:00       0
2026-05-05 02:00   4,402

options.text: The upload did not happen, since the proxy logs every web request and shows no traffic for this user in the window
The user deliberately bypassed the proxy, which proves evasion and justifies suspending the account immediately
The proxy blocked the upload, which explains why no allowed request from this user was logged in the window
The proxy feed was down for everyone, so its silence proves nothing; log the gap and get the proxy's own logs

explanation.correct: The hourly count drops to zero for all users at 23:00 and recovers at 02:00: the feed stopped, not just this user's traffic. A missing record during a collection gap is not evidence that the activity did not happen. Treat the endpoint DLP alert, which reports the upload as allowed, as the primary evidence; note the gap in the case; ask the proxy team for the appliance's local or cloud-console logs for 23:00-02:00 if they still exist; and check other sources such as firewall flows for the device. Then fix the monitoring: an alert when a source goes silent would have flagged this at 23:00, and the root cause (collector outage, expired certificate, full disk) should be tracked.

distractors.a: The empty result reflects the outage, not the user's behaviour; the zero applies to every user.
distractors.b: Nothing shows that this user bypassed anything, because everyone's proxy logs vanished at the same time. Suspension is also a containment decision that needs evidence and the agreed escalation path.
distractors.c: Blocked requests are normally logged too, with a block action, and a block for one user would not empty the whole feed.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you check the health of a source before treating its silence as evidence.

references.title: Monitor the health of your data connectors (Microsoft Sentinel)
MITRE ATT&CK T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage

questions.question: Put in order the stages a single firewall event passes through, from the device to an analyst's queue.

options.text: A correlation rule matches it together with events from other sources
The collector receives the event from the firewall over syslog
An alert is created and lands in the triage queue
Vendor field names are mapped to the common schema
The parser extracts fields such as source IP, destination and action from the raw message

explanation.correct: Collection gets the raw event into the platform (by agent, syslog or API). Parsing turns raw text into fields. Normalisation maps those fields to the common schema so one rule works across vendors (SrcIpAddr in Microsoft Sentinel ASIM, src in the Splunk CIM). Correlation evaluates normalised events from several sources against detection logic, and only then is an alert raised for triage. Some platforms normalise at query time rather than at ingestion, but logically the step still sits after parsing and before the rule. When an expected alert does not appear, walk the same chain from the start: did the event arrive, was it parsed, was it mapped, did the rule see it?

references.title: NIST SP 800-92, Guide to Computer Security Log Management
Normalization and the Advanced Security Information Model (ASIM)

questions.question: You are building the timeline for a suspected data leak at a bank in Bucharest, on a June day when local time is UTC+3. Each source writes time differently, as shown in the context. Put the events in the order they actually happened.
questions.context:
How each source writes time:
- VPN appliance: local time, no offset
- Identity provider: UTC (Z)
- Endpoint DLP: ISO 8601 with offset
- Email gateway: local time, no offset
- Web proxy: UTC (Z)

Events on 12 June 2026:
- Web proxy: 09:41:05Z upload of 380 MB to a file-sharing site
- Email gateway: 12:15:30 message with a .zip attachment to a personal address
- Endpoint DLP: 2026-06-12T11:58:00+03:00 file copied to a USB drive
- Identity provider: 08:50:12Z sign-in to the cloud file storage
- VPN appliance: 11:47:40 VPN session started

options.text: Email gateway: message with a .zip attachment to a personal address
Endpoint DLP: file copied to a USB drive
Web proxy: upload of 380 MB to a file-sharing site
VPN appliance: VPN session started
Identity provider: sign-in to the cloud file storage

explanation.correct: Convert everything to UTC first. The local-time sources need 3 hours subtracted: VPN 11:47:40 becomes 08:47:40Z and email 12:15:30 becomes 09:15:30Z. The endpoint's +03:00 offset gives 08:58:00Z. Identity and proxy are already UTC. Order: VPN session (08:47:40), cloud sign-in (08:50:12), USB copy (08:58:00), email (09:15:30), proxy upload (09:41:05). Sorting the raw values would put the sign-in and the proxy upload first and tell a different story. NIST SP 800-92 notes that organisations with systems in several time zones need to convert logged times to one zone; ASD/CISA guidance prefers UTC because it has no time zones and no daylight saving. Record each source's time zone at onboarding so the parser stores UTC and nobody has to do this arithmetic mid-incident.

references.title: ASD/CISA, Best practices for event logging and threat detection (timestamp consistency)
NIST SP 800-92, Guide to Computer Security Log Management

questions.question: Match each investigation question about a possible data leak to the log source that answers it most directly.

left.text: Which website did the user upload 40 MB to, and what category is it?
Was the message to the personal address delivered, and what was attached?
Which process wrote the file to a removable drive?
Who created an 'anyone with the link' share on the project folder?
Did the account sign in from a new country or device just before the activity?

right.text: Identity provider sign-in logs
Web proxy / secure web gateway logs
Cloud storage / SaaS audit log
Email gateway / message trace
Endpoint telemetry (EDR or endpoint DLP)
Firewall flow records

explanation.correct: Each channel has an authoritative source. Web uploads: the proxy or secure web gateway (URL, category, user, bytes; with TLS inspection, also file details). Email: the gateway or message trace (recipients, attachments, delivery status). Removable media: endpoint telemetry, which ties a file write to a process and a device. Cloud sharing: the platform's audit log (for example AnonymousLinkCreated in Microsoft 365 for an 'Anyone' link). Account context: identity provider sign-ins (location, device, MFA). Firewall flow records are the fallback when a richer source is missing: they confirm a connection and its volume, but not what was sent.

distractors.l1: Firewall flow records give IP addresses, ports and bytes, but not the URL or the site's category; the proxy logs URL, user and category.
distractors.l4: Proxy logs may show the user browsing the storage site, but only the service's own audit log records the sharing operation itself.

references.title: Microsoft Purview: audit log activities
MITRE ATT&CK data components

questions.question: True or false: when a new SOC can onboard only a few log sources in its first phase, it should start with the sources that produce the most events, because more events mean more evidence.

options.text: True
False

explanation.correct: False. Volume measures cost, not value. First-phase sources are chosen by what they let you detect and investigate for the threats that matter most, typically identity (domain controllers, identity provider sign-ins), endpoint telemetry (EDR), email, internet-facing and remote-access systems such as VPN, and cloud audit/control-plane logs. Joint ASD/CISA logging guidance prioritises sources by how likely the asset is to be targeted and how severe the impact would be if it were compromised. Some of the noisiest sources, such as verbose firewall allow logs or debug-level application logs, cost the most and add the least to first-phase detections.

distractors.a: High-volume sources are often the least valuable per event; starting with them spends the budget while key sources such as identity and EDR are still missing.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can justify an onboarding order by detection value rather than by what is easiest or biggest.

references.title: ASD/CISA, Best practices for event logging and threat detection (centralised log collection priorities)

questions.subtopic: Filtering at collection and data gaps
questions.question: True or false: once a collector filter has dropped events before ingestion to save cost, you usually cannot get those past events back for an investigation unless they were also sent to an archive.

options.text: True
False

explanation.correct: True. Most sources do not keep history for long. Windows event logs overwrite the oldest entries when they reach their size limit, network devices keep small local buffers, and SaaS audit APIs offer only a limited window (the Office 365 Management Activity API, for example, lists content from at most 7 days back). Some platforms keep longer history in their own portal (Microsoft 365 Audit Standard keeps 180 days), but that is a manual export, not a re-ingest you can rely on. Treat collector filters as a risk decision: document what is dropped and why, send the dropped stream to low-cost storage where it might matter for investigations, and review the filters when detections change.

distractors.b: This assumes the sources keep a full history that the SIEM can re-collect. Most keep days or less, and anything older is lost unless it was archived.

references.title: Office 365 Management Activity API reference
ASD/CISA, Best practices for event logging and threat detection (event log retention)

questions.question: A team maps all its firewall, proxy and DNS sources to one common schema. Which TWO benefits does this actually deliver? (Choose 2)

options.text: Fields a device never logged, such as the user on a firewall that does not record it, become available
One detection rule can run across several vendors' devices without being rewritten for each
Wrong timestamps from badly configured devices are corrected automatically
Raw events no longer need to be stored, because the normalised fields replace them
A newly onboarded source mapped to the schema is covered by existing normalised rules

explanation.correct: Normalisation gives the same thing the same name and format across sources, so detection content is written once: a rule on the normalised source-IP or URL field covers every mapped firewall or proxy, and a source added later inherits that content as soon as its parser maps to the schema. Microsoft Sentinel ASIM describes exactly these two benefits (cross-source detection and source-agnostic content); Splunk CIM, Elastic ECS and OCSF follow the same idea. Normalisation cannot create data that was never logged or fix a clock that was wrong; those problems have to be solved at the source or with enrichment.

distractors.a: Mapping renames and reformats existing fields; it cannot invent a value the source never captured. Enrichment from other sources (such as IP-to-user mapping) is a separate step with its own error rate.
distractors.c: A wrong timestamp mapped to the normalised time field is still wrong; clock and time-zone problems must be fixed at the source or in the parser.
distractors.d: Keep the raw event: parsers have bugs, schemas change, and investigators may need the original record. ASIM's query-time parsers, for example, deliberately leave the source data unmodified.

references.title: Normalization and the Advanced Security Information Model (ASIM)
Elastic Common Schema (ECS) reference

questions.question: Which events does the Sigma selection below match?
questions.context:
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 4663
    ObjectName|contains:
      - '\Payroll\'
      - '\Board\'
  condition: selection

options.text: Event 4663 where the object path contains both \Payroll\ and \Board\
Any event with ID 4663, plus any event whose path contains either folder name
Event 4663 where the object path contains \Payroll\ or \Board\
Event 4663 where the object path is exactly \Payroll\ or exactly \Board\

explanation.correct: Sigma builds AND and OR from the YAML structure. Keys inside one selection map (EventID and ObjectName) are joined with AND; the items of a list under one field are joined with OR. The selection therefore means EventID = 4663 AND (ObjectName contains \Payroll\ OR ObjectName contains \Board\). Event 4663 ('an attempt was made to access an object') is only logged where object-access auditing and a SACL are set on the folder, so the rule also depends on that audit configuration.

distractors.a: Requiring both values needs the |all modifier (ObjectName|contains|all); a plain list is OR.
distractors.b: Fields in the same selection map are ANDed. An OR between them would need two selections joined with 'or' in the condition.
distractors.d: The |contains modifier makes it a substring match; without a modifier the value would be compared exactly.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you read Sigma YAML precisely, because one misread list or modifier changes what the rule catches.

references.title: Sigma documentation: Rules
Sigma documentation: Modifiers

questions.question: A detection engineer at a security software vendor adds the line 'Backup job run by svc_backup' under the falsepositives field of a Sigma rule, converts the rule and deploys it. Alerts for svc_backup keep arriving. What explains this, and what is the fix?

options.text: The account must be written as CORP\svc_backup so the converter turns that entry into an exclusion
falsepositives is documentation only; add a filter selection for svc_backup and use 'selection and not filter'
The account belongs in the logsource section (service: svc_backup) so the converter scopes the rule away from it
Converters apply falsepositives entries only to rules whose level is low or medium, so lower the level first

explanation.correct: Sigma converters do not parse the falsepositives field; it tells the analyst when the rule may fire for benign reasons. Exclusions must be part of the detection logic: add a selection such as filter_backup (User: 'CORP\svc_backup', ideally combined with the backup tool's path or parent process so the exclusion stays narrow) and change the condition to 'selection and not filter_backup'. Sigma Filters, kept in separate files, are another way to apply environment-specific exclusions without editing the original rule. After the change, replay the rule to confirm the backup job no longer alerts and the same activity from another account still does.

distractors.a: Formatting the name differently does not help; the converter ignores the falsepositives field whatever it contains.
distractors.c: logsource selects which log data the rule searches (category, product, service); putting an account there breaks log-source matching instead of excluding it.
distractors.d: level only describes criticality; no level value makes a converter read the falsepositives field.

explanation.interview_angle: Separating rule documentation from rule logic, a common mistake when people first adapt community Sigma rules.

references.title: Sigma documentation: Rules
Sigma documentation: Filters

E2 only
E2 and E4, because both copy data to a mega: remote
E2, E3 and E4, because only svc_backup is excluded

explanation.correct: The condition needs both selections (all of selection_*: Image ends with \rclone.exe AND the command line contains ' copy ' or ' sync ') and no match on filter_backup. filter_backup is a map, so it excludes only events where User is CORP\svc_backup AND the parent ends with \backupagent.exe. E1 matches both selections and the whole filter, so it is suppressed. E2 is the same account launched from cmd.exe; the filter does not match, so it alerts, which is exactly the case an attacker who stole the backup account would create. E3 has neither copy nor sync. E4 is rclone renamed to svchost.exe in Temp: Image|endswith fails, so this rule is blind to it. Cover that gap with a detection that does not depend on the file name, for example the copy-to-remote command-line pattern or the binary's hash from EDR.

distractors.a: E1 is suppressed: both fields of filter_backup (User and ParentImage) match, and a Sigma map is AND, so the filter removes exactly this combination.
distractors.c: E4 fails selection_img because the renamed binary does not end with \rclone.exe; it is the rule's blind spot, not an alert.
distractors.d: E3 runs 'rclone.exe config', which contains neither ' copy ' nor ' sync ', and E4 fails selection_img; only E2 satisfies every part of the condition.

explanation.interview_angle: Reading a rule as an attacker would: which exclusion still alerts on abuse of the excluded account, and which simple rename evades it.

questions.question: A detection engineer at a security vendor converts a community Sigma rule (logsource process_creation on windows, fields Image and CommandLine) into the SIEM's query language. In a lab, the exact command runs on a monitored host and the process-creation event is visible in the SIEM, but the converted query returns nothing. What should be checked first?

options.text: The rule's level, because converters drop rules that are marked medium or lower
Whether the rule should be rewritten as a keyword search over the raw event text
Whether the SIEM batches process-creation events, so the test is repeated after a day
Whether the converted field names and log source match this SIEM's data

explanation.correct: Sigma field names are generic (Image, CommandLine), but each SIEM stores process creation in its own table or index with its own field names. If the event is in the SIEM yet the query finds nothing, the usual cause is that the converted query looks in the wrong place or for fields that do not exist there. pySigma handles this with processing pipelines (field_name_mapping, plus conditions that point the query at the right index or source). Compare the converted query with a sample event: Windows Security event 4688 stores the path as NewProcessName and records the command line only when 'Include command line in process creation events' is enabled, while an EDR table such as DeviceProcessEvents uses FolderPath and ProcessCommandLine. Fix the mapping, then rerun the lab test.

distractors.a: level only states criticality; it does not stop a converter from producing a query or the query from matching.
distractors.b: A raw keyword search might return the event, but it is slower and less precise, and it hides the mapping problem instead of fixing it.
distractors.c: The event is already searchable in the SIEM, so ingestion timing is not why the query misses it.

explanation.interview_angle: Knowing that a Sigma rule is only as good as its field mapping in your environment, the main reason imported rules fail silently.

questions.question: Put the stages of a detection use case's lifecycle in order.

options.text: Tune the logic and exclusions using analyst feedback and alert metrics
Design: define the threat behaviour, the log sources needed and the expected analyst response
Retire or rebuild the rule when its data source or threat no longer applies, and update the use-case register
Test the rule against historical data and a simulated true positive
Deploy the rule to production with a severity, an owner and a runbook
Build the rule logic and document known false positives and blind spots

explanation.correct: A use case starts with design (what behaviour, which data, what the analyst should do), then the rule is built and documented, tested before anyone is paged, deployed with an owner and runbook, tuned from real alert outcomes, and finally retired or rebuilt when its data source or the threat changes. Tuning and re-testing repeat during the rule's life, but the first test always comes before deployment, and retirement is recorded in the register so coverage reports stay honest. Palantir's Alerting and Detection Strategy (ADS) template, for example, requires goal, ATT&CK categorisation, blind spots, false positives, validation and response sections before a rule goes to production.
explanation.interview_angle: Whether you treat detections as maintained products with an owner and an end of life, not as one-off queries.

questions.question: An MSSP client complains that one rule produces 150 alerts a day, almost all benign. Put the tuning steps in order.

options.text: Write the narrowest exclusion that matches that pattern, combining fields such as account, host and process path
Export the rule's alerts and their closure reasons for the last 30 days
Replay the tuned rule over the same period and over saved true-positive samples to confirm they still fire
Group the benign alerts by shared attributes to find the dominant pattern
Release the change through version control with a ticket, owner and review date, then watch the alert volume

explanation.correct: Tuning starts with evidence: the alert history and how analysts closed each alert. Grouping the benign alerts shows which pattern produces most of the noise (often one service account, host or parent process). Only then is an exclusion written, as narrow as possible and combining several fields, so an attacker cannot reuse a single excluded value. Before release, replay the tuned rule over the same period (the noise should drop) and over known true-positive samples (they must still fire). Finally ship it like code, with a ticket, owner and review date, and watch the volume afterwards. In Microsoft Sentinel the exclusion list can live in a watchlist read with _GetWatchlist(), so it is managed centrally without editing every rule.
explanation.interview_angle: Whether your tuning is measured and regression-tested, not a guess that quietly removes detection.

questions.question: Match each detection rule to the ATT&CK technique it should be mapped to.

left.text: Outbound uploads from one host split into many near-identical 90 MB requests, each just under the proxy's 100 MB alert threshold
A file server sends data to the same external address at 03:00 every night, outside any approved backup or batch job
A workstation process uploads several gigabytes to a consumer file-hosting service
One source tries the same common password against hundreds of different accounts

right.text: T1110.003 Password Spraying
T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
T1029 Scheduled Transfer
T1030 Data Transfer Size Limits
T1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
T1078 Valid Accounts

explanation.correct: Map a rule to the behaviour it actually observes. Fixed-size chunks kept below a threshold are the defining trait of T1030 Data Transfer Size Limits. Transfers tied to a fixed time of day are T1029 Scheduled Transfer. Uploads to a cloud storage or file-hosting service are T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage. One password tried against many accounts is T1110.003 Password Spraying. In Sigma the mapping goes in tags (for example attack.exfiltration and attack.t1567.002); in a Microsoft Sentinel analytics rule it is set in the tactics and techniques fields, which feed the MITRE coverage view.

distractors.l4: T1078 Valid Accounts describes using an account after the spray succeeds; this rule detects the guessing itself.

questions.question: A bank's use-case register lists 'Brute force against legacy VPN' as active coverage for T1110 and T1133. The legacy VPN was decommissioned eight months ago, the rule has produced no alerts since, and the new remote-access platform logs in a different format. The register feeds the quarterly detection-coverage report to management. What is the correct action?

options.text: Keep the use case listed as active, because eight months with no alerts shows that no brute-force attempts reached the bank
Delete the rule from the SIEM to tidy up the content, since the platform it was watching no longer exists
Re-point the existing rule's tags to the new remote-access platform so the quarterly coverage figure stays unchanged
Retire it formally, record the gap in the register and report, and open a change to rebuild it on the new logs

explanation.correct: A rule whose data source no longer exists detects nothing, so listing it as coverage misstates the bank's detection capability to management. The right move is a documented retirement: mark the use case retired in the register with reason and date, show the gap in the coverage report, and raise a change to rebuild the detection on the new platform's logs (onboarding, parsing, field mapping, testing) with a named owner and target date. For an EU financial entity this is more than hygiene: DORA art. 10 expects detection mechanisms to be in place and regularly tested, so a stale register is an audit finding waiting to happen.

distractors.a: Zero alerts here means zero input: the source was switched off. Silence from a rule with no data says nothing about attacks.
distractors.b: Silent deletion loses the audit trail and leaves remote-access attacks uncovered with nobody tasked to fix it.
distractors.c: Changing labels without changing logic or data overstates coverage; the rule still cannot read the new platform's logs.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you keep the use-case inventory honest, because coverage numbers reach management and auditors.

questions.question: Internal audit at an EU bank asks the SOC for evidence that its detection mechanisms are regularly tested, as DORA requires. Which evidence actually answers the request?

options.text: A per-use-case record of periodic true-positive tests: date, method, rule version, result and fixes
Dashboards showing that every enabled rule produced at least one alert during the last quarter, with volumes per rule
The ATT&CK heatmap showing which techniques have at least one enabled rule mapped to them, grouped by tactic
The SIEM vendor's written statement that its built-in rule templates are quality-tested before each release

explanation.correct: DORA art. 10(1) requires financial entities to have mechanisms that promptly detect anomalous activities and says all of them shall be regularly tested (in accordance with art. 25); art. 10(2) adds defined alert thresholds and criteria that trigger incident response. A test means deliberately producing the behaviour and checking that the rule fires and the alert reaches the right queue. The evidence is therefore a record per use case: when it was tested, how (for example an Atomic Red Team test or a scripted simulation on a test host), which rule version, whether it fired, and what was fixed when it did not. This is the Validation section of an ADS-style use case, kept current.

distractors.b: Alerts firing shows activity, not detection quality: they may all be false positives, and a broken rule that stopped firing is invisible on this view.
distractors.c: A mapping is a claim about intent; it does not show the rule works on the bank's data, fields and exclusions.
distractors.d: The vendor tests the template, not your parsing, field names, exclusions and data sources, which is where rules usually break.

explanation.interview_angle: Separating 'we have rules' from 'we can prove they detect', which is what auditors and supervisors probe.
