questions.question: True or false: a vendor's detection team replays a new rule over 30 days of production data and gets zero results; this shows the rule works, so it can be enabled without further testing.

options.text: True
False

explanation.correct: False. A quiet backtest only shows the rule will not flood the queue; it cannot tell 'no attack happened' from 'the logic or field names are broken'. Before production you also need a positive test: reproduce the behaviour (for example with an Atomic Red Team test or a scripted simulation on a lab host), confirm the expected events reach the SIEM with the fields the rule uses, and check that the rule fires. The ADS framework calls this true-positive validation and treats a rule that cannot be made to fire as one to refactor or discard. Microsoft Sentinel's 'Test with current data' in the rule wizard shows how often the rule would have fired on current data: useful for volume, but still not a positive test.

distractors.a: Zero hits is equally consistent with a broken rule; volume testing and detection testing answer different questions.

questions.question: An MSSP onboards a client whose firewall logs reach the SIEM through an on-premises collector and arrive up to 4 minutes after the event time. A scheduled rule runs every 5 minutes over events whose event time falls in the last 5 minutes. Testing shows that some matching events never alert. Which change closes the gap without creating duplicate alerts?

options.text: Widen the look-back to 9 minutes on event time, so late events fall inside the next run's window
Run the rule every minute over the last minute of event time, so events are checked sooner
Widen the look-back to 9 minutes on event time and keep only events ingested in the last 5 minutes
Run the rule hourly over the last hour of event time, so the delay is small next to the window

explanation.correct: An event generated at minute 4 but ingested at minute 7 is not in the SIEM when the first run executes, and by the second run its event time is outside the 5-minute window, so it is never evaluated. The fix is to look back over interval plus maximum delay (5 + 4 = 9 minutes) on event time, and to assign each event to exactly one run by keeping only events ingested since the previous run. Microsoft documents this pattern for Sentinel scheduled rules: where TimeGenerated >= ago(9m) | where ingestion_time() > ago(5m). Measure the real delay per source first (TimeGenerated against ingestion_time()) rather than guessing. In Splunk the same idea uses the index time (_indextime) alongside the event time.

distractors.a: This catches late events, but the overlapping windows evaluate many events twice, so one activity can raise two alerts.
distractors.b: A 1-minute window is shorter than the 4-minute delay, so even more events arrive after their window has passed.
distractors.d: Events from the last minutes of each hour still arrive after the run, and every detection is delayed by up to an hour.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you understand that the SIEM sees events when they are ingested, not when they happened, and how that silently breaks scheduled rules.

questions.question: A bank's rule flags Tier-0 admin sign-ins outside 07:00-19:00. Change CHG-2291 was meant to suppress only the vulnerability scanner's service account when it signs in from the scanner host. What does the added line actually do?

options.text: It suppresses only events where the account is svc_vulnscan and the source is 198.51.100.20, as intended
It suppresses all svc_vulnscan sign-ins from any address and all sign-ins from 198.51.100.20
It suppresses nothing, because both inequality checks must fail at the same time for a row to be dropped
It suppresses only sign-ins from 198.51.100.20; the account check has no effect on the result

explanation.correct: where keeps a row only when the whole expression is true. 'Account != X and SourceIP != Y' is true only when both values differ, so a row is dropped as soon as either the account is svc_vulnscan or the IP is 198.51.100.20 (De Morgan: not(A or B) = not A and not B). That silences two things the bank still needs to see: the scanner's privileged account used from anywhere else (stolen credentials) and any other admin signing in from the scanner host. To exclude only the pair, write | where not(Account == "svc_vulnscan" and SourceIP == "198.51.100.20"); in SPL, NOT (user="svc_vulnscan" AND src_ip="198.51.100.20"). Keep the pair in a watchlist or lookup, and replay the rule with a test sign-in by svc_vulnscan from another IP to prove it still fires.

distractors.a: That needs not(Account == ... and SourceIP == ...); the line as written drops a row when either value matches.
distractors.c: A row is dropped when the expression is false, which happens as soon as one value matches; it suppresses more, not nothing.
distractors.d: The account check works on its own: svc_vulnscan from any IP is dropped too, not only traffic from that address.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can spot an exclusion that is wider than its change ticket says, a classic way tuning creates blind spots.

questions.question: A bank's 'large upload to cloud storage' rule fires every working day at 16:00 for three Treasury users who upload a 1.2 GB position file to the bank's own tenant of a SaaS storage service, as a documented process requires. What tuning should the L2 analyst recommend?

options.text: Raise the rule's threshold for all users from 500 MB to 2 GB so the daily position file no longer triggers it
Exclude the Treasury department from the rule, since its staff move large files every day as part of the job
Lower the rule's severity to informational so these alerts stop paging analysts but stay searchable
Allowlist only the pair of the bank's tenant ID and those three accounts, with an owner and review date

explanation.correct: The noise has one precise cause, three known accounts sending to the bank's own tenant, so the exception should match exactly that combination and nothing more. Identify the destination by tenant (tenant ID or tenant-specific hostname), not by the service's domain: the same domain also serves personal and third-party tenants, which is exactly where exfiltration would go. Keep the pair in a reviewed allowlist (for example a Sentinel watchlist or a Splunk lookup) with an owner and review date, and replay the rule to confirm that an upload by a Treasury user to a personal tenant still fires.

distractors.a: A global threshold change creates a blind spot for every user between 500 MB and 2 GB, and the file will eventually outgrow 2 GB.
distractors.b: Treasury handles some of the bank's most sensitive data; excluding the department removes coverage where an insider would do the most damage.
distractors.c: The alerts still land in the queue, and a real exfiltration by these users would now be buried as informational.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether your tuning removes the noise without opening a door, especially for sanctioned SaaS destinations.

questions.question: An MSSP client announces an authorised vulnerability scan from 203.0.113.50 this Saturday 22:00 to Sunday 04:00 that will trip several network rules. What should the SOC do?

options.text: Add an exception for that IP and window only, citing the approval, that expires after the scan
Add a permanent exclusion for 203.0.113.50 to every affected rule so that this vendor's future scans never alert again
Disable the affected rules from Saturday evening and re-enable them on Monday morning once the scan report arrives
Leave the rules unchanged and ask the night shift to close every alert from the scan as a false positive

explanation.correct: The scan is authorised, time-bound and from a known source, so the exception should be too: scope it to the source IP and the agreed window, record the client's approval, auto-close matching alerts with that reason, and let it expire. Anything from another source, or from that IP outside the window, still alerts. In Microsoft Sentinel this is an automation rule created from the incident, with conditions on the IP and an expiration date; it keeps an audit trail and leaves the analytics rule untouched.

distractors.b: A permanent exclusion leaves a lasting blind spot: if the scanner host or the vendor's address is later abused, nothing alerts.
distractors.c: Disabling the rules blinds the SOC to everything they detect, from every source, for the whole weekend.
distractors.d: This floods the night queue, risks burying a real alert, and labels expected activity as false positives, which skews tuning metrics.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you suppress expected noise with scope, a time limit and an audit trail instead of switching detection off.

questions.question: At an MSSP, a client's rule detects new mailbox rules that forward mail to an external domain. The analyst confirms that an executive assistant created one, with documented approval, to forward invoices to the external auditors. How should the alert be classified so the tuning data stays accurate?

options.text: False positive, because no malicious activity took place and the user did nothing wrong
True positive, escalated to incident response as a confirmed leak of company data
Benign positive, with the approval reference recorded in the closing comment
Undetermined, because the forwarding rule is still active in the mailbox today

explanation.correct: The rule did exactly what it was built for: it saw a new external forwarding rule. The activity is suspicious by design but authorised, which is a benign positive (Microsoft Sentinel's closing classification 'Benign Positive - suspicious but expected'). Engineers read false positives as 'the logic or the data is wrong' and respond by narrowing the rule; labelling this one a false positive invites an exclusion that could blind the rule to the next, malicious forwarding rule. With the approval reference in the comment, a permanent arrangement can also justify a narrow, reviewed allowlist entry.

distractors.a: False positive means the rule matched something it should not have (wrong logic or wrong data); here it matched precisely what it was designed to catch.
distractors.b: Nothing indicates misuse; the forwarding is approved, so opening an incident wastes response time.
distractors.d: The facts are established (who, why, approval); undetermined is for alerts that could not be resolved.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you know closure codes are tuning data, and that benign positives and false positives lead to different fixes.

questions.question: Which aggregation lets a rule detect password spraying, where one source tries one or two passwords against many different accounts?

options.text: Count failed logons per account in a 10-minute window and alert when one account exceeds 10
Sum the bytes sent per source IP in a 10-minute window and alert above a volume limit
Count successful logons per account per day and alert when a day exceeds the user's average
Count distinct accounts with failed logons per source IP in a window, alert above a limit

explanation.correct: Spraying keeps the attempts per account low (often one or two) to avoid lockouts, so the signal is breadth: one source failing against many accounts. The rule therefore groups by source and counts distinct target accounts. In KQL on event 4625: summarize dcount(TargetUserName) by IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m); in SPL: stats dc(user) by src_ip; in Sigma, a value_count correlation grouped by the source. A useful follow-up is any success (4624) from the same source after the burst.

distractors.a: This catches brute force against one account; a sprayer stays at one or two failures per account and never reaches 10.
distractors.b: Logon attempts carry almost no data, so byte volume says nothing about password guessing.
distractors.c: Successful logons measure normal use; a spray is mostly failures spread across many accounts.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you choose the grouping key and count type from the attack's shape, not from habit.

questions.question: At a bank, one rule alerts whenever any employee uploads more than 1 GB in a day. Traders routinely move several gigabytes, while call-centre agents rarely exceed 50 MB. What is the main weakness of this rule?

options.text: It is noisy for heavy users yet blind to an agent sending 900 MB, as normal volume differs by role
A fixed limit cannot be expressed in most SIEM query languages, so the rule will behave unreliably
1 GB is too low for a modern bank and should simply be raised to 10 GB for everyone
Monitoring upload volume per employee is not permitted under GDPR, so the rule should be removed entirely

explanation.correct: One number cannot fit groups whose normal behaviour differs by two orders of magnitude: traders trigger it daily (noise), while an agent sending 900 MB, about 18 times their normal, never does (blind spot). Baselining fixes this by comparing each user with their own history and with a peer group, for example alerting when today's volume exceeds a multiple of the user's 95th percentile of daily totals over 30 days and is far above peers, with an absolute ceiling kept as a backstop. In KQL, percentile(DailyBytes, 95) by user builds the baseline; in SPL, stats perc95(daily_bytes) by user.

distractors.b: A fixed threshold is trivial to express (where bytes > limit); the problem is what the number means, not syntax.
distractors.c: A higher global number cuts trader noise but makes the blind spot for low-volume roles much larger.
distractors.d: GDPR requires a lawful basis, proportionality and transparency for such monitoring (recital 49 recognises network and information security as a legitimate interest); it does not forbid this rule.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can explain why per-user and peer baselines beat a single global threshold.

questions.question: A post-incident review at a bank finds that a departing employee moved client files to a personal cloud account over six weeks, raising daily uploads gradually from 50 MB to 2 GB. The anomaly rule alerts when a day's volume exceeds 3 times the user's rolling 14-day average. It never fired. What explains this, and what is the best fix?

options.text: The multiplier was too high; lowering it from 3x to 2x for all users would have caught the gradual increase in time
The rolling average rose with the uploads; add a fixed earlier reference period, peer comparison and a ceiling
The baseline was too long; comparing each day with the previous day alone would have reacted faster
The uploads used HTTPS, so the proxy could not measure their volume without TLS inspection

explanation.correct: A slow ramp drags the baseline along with it. Going from 50 MB to 2 GB over about 42 days is roughly 9 % growth a day; against a 14-day rolling average, each day sits at under 2 times the baseline, so a 3x rule never fires, even though the last day is 40 times the starting level. Designs that resist this drift: compare with a reference period that does not move with recent activity (for example the same user 60-90 days earlier), compare with same-role peers, keep an absolute ceiling, and add context such as resignation status and a personal cloud destination. Microsoft Sentinel UEBA, for example, scores activity against both the entity's own history and its peer group.

distractors.a: At about 9 % daily growth the ratio to a 14-day average stays below 2x, so 2x would still miss it, while noise rises for everyone.
distractors.c: Day-over-day growth was only about 9 %, far below any useful multiplier; a shorter baseline drifts even faster.
distractors.d: Proxies log byte counts per connection without decrypting TLS; the volume was visible, it was judged against a drifting baseline.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you understand that an insider can 'train' a rolling baseline, and how to design detections against it.

questions.question: A post-incident review finds that an attacker uploaded a 6 GB archive to an uncategorised domain as 190 MB parts over two hours. The exfiltration rule alerts when a single outbound request to an uncategorised domain exceeds 200 MB. Which change to the detection logic would have caught this while keeping the rule's intent?

options.text: Sum bytes per host and destination over a few hours and alert on the total, keeping the per-request check
Lower the per-request threshold to 100 MB so that parts of this size would trigger the rule next time
Alert on every HTTPS connection to an uncategorised domain, regardless of how much data is actually sent
Alert only when the destination domain also appears on a commercial threat-intelligence blocklist feed

explanation.correct: Splitting data into pieces below a known threshold is ATT&CK T1030 Data Transfer Size Limits, and any per-event threshold invites it. Aggregating per source and destination over time measures what matters, the total that left. In KQL: summarize sum(SentBytes) by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h), or a longer look-back for a sliding view; in SPL: stats sum(bytes_out) by src, dest over the window. Keep the per-request check as well, so a single huge upload still alerts at once, and keep the uncategorised or first-seen destination condition so the volume rule stays precise.

distractors.b: The attacker simply picks smaller parts; a lower per-request limit adds noise without closing the gap.
distractors.c: Uncategorised domains are common in normal browsing; without a volume condition this floods the queue and loses the exfiltration signal.
distractors.d: Fresh attacker infrastructure is rarely on blocklists in time; this narrows the rule to known-bad and still misses this case.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you think about how attackers shape activity around known thresholds and aggregate accordingly.

questions.question: A correlation rule at a bank raises the alert below. Which reading of it is correct?
questions.context:
Alert EXFIL-CORR-07  Anomalous upload to new destination  score 4/4
user=d.stan (Payments Operations)  host=WS-PAY-118 (managed laptop)
window=2026-03-14 (Saturday) 01:52-02:41 local  user usual activity: Mon-Fri 08:30-17:30
proxy: POST share.example.net  category=Uncategorized  bytes_out=3.6 GB in 412 requests
baseline: user 30-day p95 = 150 MB/day
first_seen: destination not contacted by any host in the previous 90 days
auth: VPN session 01:47 from 203.0.113.77 (ISP seen for this user before), MFA approved

options.text: It proves that payments data was exfiltrated by d.stan, so the regulatory notification clock has started
It is probably benign: the laptop is managed and MFA was approved, which together rule out account misuse
It shows a strong behavioural anomaly for the account, but not which files left or who was at the keyboard
The first-seen signal should be discounted, because new uncategorised domains appear every day

explanation.correct: Each signal is weak alone, but together they are strong: 3.6 GB is about 24 times the user's p95, sent on a Saturday night outside the user's normal hours, to a destination nobody in the bank has used in 90 days. What the alert does not show is content (bytes_out is volume, not data type) or identity beyond the account (an approved MFA prompt does not prove the user was acting: MFA fatigue, a stolen session or a shared device are possible). The L2 next steps are evidence, not conclusions: endpoint and DLP file events on WS-PAY-118 for 01:52-02:41 (which files were read or archived), the VPN and sign-in details, the destination's ownership, and any approved change or business reason. Containment and escalation follow from what that shows, and any regulatory assessment needs to know what data left.

questions.question: An alert reports that a user uploaded 700 MB to a web destination. Which TWO additional facts most raise the likelihood that this is exfiltration rather than normal work? (Choose 2)

The upload happened on a weekday, well within the user's normal working hours
The volume is about 20 times the user's own 30-day daily 95th percentile
The destination is the company's sanctioned cloud storage tenant

In KQL, first-seen is typically a join kind=leftanti against the destinations seen in the history window, and the baseline is a per-user percentile of daily totals. questions.question: Which TWO situations commonly produce impossible-travel alerts that are not account compromise? (Choose 2)

The user's traffic exits through a corporate VPN or cloud proxy whose egress IP geolocates to another country

An IP geolocation database places a mobile carrier's address in the wrong city or country
One IP address fails sign-ins against many different accounts

questions.question: A SaaS company's detection team wants an alert when a host uploads more than 50 MB to a domain no host contacted in the previous 30 days. The hourly rule builds a list of known domains from the last 30 days of proxy logs up to now, then keeps last-hour uploads whose domain is not in that list. In testing it never fires, even when a tester uploads 200 MB to a brand-new domain. Why?

options.text: The history includes the hour being tested, so each new domain is already in the known list
Thirty days is too short a history; the known list needs at least 90 days of data to be reliable
The known list must be built per host, because an organisation-wide list hides domains new to one host
The 50 MB threshold should apply to each request, not to the total per host and domain

explanation.correct: The 'known' set must describe the past only. Built over the last 30 days up to now, it includes the hour under test, so any domain used in that hour counts as known and the anti-join removes everything. End the history where the detection window starts: let known = Proxy | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1h)) | distinct DestinationHost; then join the last hour's per-host totals to it with kind=leftanti on DestinationHost. In SPL the same idea is stats earliest(_time) as first_seen by dest over 30 days, keeping destinations whose first_seen falls inside the last hour. At scale, keep the history in a summary table or lookup refreshed daily instead of scanning 30 days every hour.

distractors.b: A longer history makes more domains 'known'; it cannot fix a list that already contains the hour under test.
distractors.c: Per-host history is a valid design choice, but it would still include the current hour and still never fire.
distractors.d: Per-request thresholds are easier to evade with chunked uploads, and the threshold is not why the rule returns nothing.

questions.question: A detection rule is meant to catch password spraying. During a sanctioned test, one IP address tried a single password against 400 accounts in 15 minutes, yet the rule did not fire. Why?
questions.context:
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ResultType == "50126"
| summarize Attempts = count() by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| where Attempts > 20

options.text: ResultType 50126 is the code for a successful sign-in, so the filter quietly excludes every failed attempt from the count
The one-hour lookback is too short to hold a 15-minute test, so the events fall outside the window
Grouping by account and IP counts tries per account; a spray makes one per account, so no group reaches 20
Failed interactive sign-ins are written to the AuditLogs table, not SigninLogs, so the query reads the wrong table

explanation.correct: ResultType 50126 is the Entra ID code for an invalid username or password, so the filter itself is right. The flaw is the summarize: `by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress` makes one row per account-and-IP pair, and in a spray each pair holds one or two attempts, so `Attempts > 20` never matches. Spraying is wide and shallow, so the rule must measure breadth per source: `| summarize Attempts = count(), Accounts = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by IPAddress | where Accounts > 20`. In Splunk the same idea is `stats count, dc(user) as accounts by src | where accounts > 20`. As written, the query is a brute-force rule (many attempts against one account), which is why it stays silent during a spray.

distractors.a: ResultType 0 is success; 50126 is the invalid username or password failure, which is exactly what a spray produces.
distractors.b: A 15-minute burst that just ended sits inside ago(1h); a wider window would not change the one-attempt-per-account count.
distractors.d: AuditLogs holds Entra ID directory changes (users, groups, roles, apps). Interactive sign-in successes and failures are in SigninLogs.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you can tell a brute-force rule (count per account) from a spray rule (distinct accounts per source) by reading one summarize line.

questions.question: An MSSP rule should flag any source with more than 50 failed logons within a single hour. Run over 24 hours, it flags printers and kiosks that never exceed 5 failures in any hour. What is wrong with the search?
questions.context:
index=wineventlog source="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4625
| bin _time span=1h
| stats count by src
| where count > 50

options.text: bin must come after stats; placed before it, the time buckets are applied to the wrong events
_time is missing from the by clause, so stats totals each source over all 24 hours
where cannot compare a numeric field in SPL, so the last line must be rewritten as search count>50
EventCode 4625 also includes successful logons, which inflates the count for busy shared devices

explanation.correct: `bin _time span=1h` only rounds each event's _time down to the hour; the grouping happens in stats. Because the by clause lists only src, all hourly buckets for a source collapse into one 24-hour total, so a kiosk failing 3 times an hour with a stale saved password reaches 72 and fires. The fix is `| stats count by _time, src`, which gives one row per source per hour, and `where count > 50` then tests each hour. The KQL equivalent puts the bucket inside the grouping: `SecurityEvent | where EventID == 4625 | summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h), IpAddress | where count_ > 50`.

distractors.d: 4625 is "An account failed to log on"; successful logons are 4624 and are not selected by this search.

explanation.interview_angle: Reading an SPL search line by line and seeing that bucketing without grouping on _time quietly turns a per-hour rule into a per-day rule.

questions.question: A ticket asks which file a user sent to an online storage site. The web proxy has this single entry for the session. What can the analyst conclude from it?

options.text: The user uploaded one file of about 48 KB, and the name of that file can be read from the url field

The proxy decrypted and scanned the session, so the transferred content was inspected and found clean

distractors.c: For CONNECT, 200 means "tunnel established". What happened inside the tunnel, including any upload result, is invisible to the proxy.

distractors.d: The click event ends at the gateway's redirect. Credential entry would show as a POST in proxy logs or as sign-ins from unfamiliar IPs, which are not in this log.
distractors.e: The removal came after c.dinu's click, so her account still needs checking and possibly a password reset and session revocation.

explanation.interview_angle: Separating delivered, clicked and compromised: three different claims that need three different pieces of evidence.

questions.question: In a bank insider case, a hunter runs this query against a treasury workstation. Which TWO statements are correct? (Choose 2)

| where DeviceName == "wks-tr-0147.bank.example"
| where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-10-18T16:40:00Z) .. datetime(2026-10-18T17:10:00Z))
| where ActionType == "FileCreated" and FolderPath startswith @"E:\"
| summarize Files = count(), First = min(Timestamp), Last = max(Timestamp)
    by InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SensitivityLabel

InitiatingProcessFileName  InitiatingProcessAccountName  SensitivityLabel  Files  First     Last
explorer.exe               v.nistor                      Confidential      214    16:52:07  16:58:40
explorer.exe               v.nistor                      (empty)           9      16:52:10  16:53:02

options.text: Drive E: is proven to be a USB stick, because only removable drives are given letters after C:
The sensitivity labels were stripped during the copy, as the rows with an empty label show
Explorer, as v.nistor, created 223 files on E: in about six minutes, 214 labelled Confidential
To show E: was removable media, find a device-mount event for that letter on this host just before 16:52
The files have left the bank's premises, so this is a confirmed breach that is ready for regulatory reporting

explanation.correct: The summarised rows show FileCreated events under E:\ initiated by explorer.exe in v.nistor's context: 214 Confidential files plus 9 unlabelled ones between 16:52 and 16:58 (c), consistent with a drag-and-drop copy. The drive letter alone does not say what E: is: it could be a second internal disk, a mapped share or a phone. In Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, DeviceEvents records with ActionType UsbDriveMounted carry the drive letter, product name and serial number in AdditionalFields; one for E: just before 16:52 proves removable media and identifies the device to recover (d). Device-control logs serve the same purpose in other EDR tools.

distractors.b: Nothing here shows a label changing; the 9 files may simply never have been labelled. Proving label removal needs label-change audit records, not an empty column.
distractors.e: Copying to a local drive is not yet data leaving the bank. Whether the device left the premises, whether it was encrypted, and whether this is reportable all need more facts.

questions.question: A KQL hunting query filters process events with `ProcessCommandLine has "enc"` to find PowerShell started with an encoded command. Which statement about this filter is correct?

options.text: It matches -enc, -Enc and -EncodedCommand alike, because has looks for the text anywhere in the string
It misses -ENC written in upper case, because has is a case-sensitive operator
It returns nothing at all, because has cannot search for terms shorter than four characters
It matches -enc and -ENC but misses -EncodedCommand, because has only matches whole terms

explanation.correct: KQL splits strings into terms, maximal runs of alphanumeric characters, and has is true only when the right-hand side is a whole term. In "powershell -enc SQBFAFgA..." the term is enc, so it matches, case-insensitively, so -ENC too. In "-EncodedCommand" the term is EncodedCommand and "enc" is only a substring, so the row is missed, and PowerShell accepts other abbreviations as well. Use `has_any` with every known spelling, `contains`, or a regex, and test the rule against a sample of each form. The Microsoft docs give the same trap: "KustoExplorerQueryRun" has "Explorer" is false, while contains returns true.

distractors.a: That describes contains, a substring match. has is term-based and does not match part of a longer term.
distractors.b: has is case-insensitive; the case-sensitive variant is has_cs.
distractors.c: Terms shorter than three characters are not in the term index, so the query falls back to a slower scan, but it still works; "enc" has three characters anyway.

explanation.interview_angle: Whether you test a detection against every way an attacker can write the same command instead of trusting one string.

questions.question: An MSSP analyst totals a client's web uploads two ways over the same period. `index=proxy action=allowed | stats sum(bytes_out)` gives 63 GB, but `index=proxy action=allowed | stats sum(bytes_out) as up by user` adds up to only 41 GB. Some proxy nodes log unauthenticated traffic without a user field. What explains the gap?

options.text: stats leaves out events that lack the by field, so uploads with no user never reach a group
stats samples large result sets by default, so the grouped search silently reads fewer events
Naming the result with as up truncates large sums to a 32-bit integer
With a by clause, stats keeps only the first event per user and quietly discards repeat uploads

explanation.correct: When an event has no value for a by-clause field, stats does not create a group for it, so the event drops out of the grouped results (Splunk documents the same rule explicitly for tstats: rows with a null group-by field are omitted unless fillnull_value is set). Here 22 GB of uploads came from traffic with no user, and unattributed traffic is often exactly what an analyst should look at (service accounts, authentication bypass rules, malware that avoids the proxy login). `| fillnull value="unknown" user | stats sum(bytes_out) as up by user` keeps it visible as its own row. A quick habit: reconcile a grouped total against the ungrouped total before trusting a report.

distractors.b: stats processes every event the search returns; it does not sample.
distractors.c: as only names the output field, and sum() handles values far larger than 63 GB.
distractors.d: That is what dedup does. stats sum() adds every event in each group.

explanation.interview_angle: Checking that a grouped total reconciles with the ungrouped total, and knowing why it might not.

questions.question: A hunter at a SaaS vendor investigates suspected token theft. Exchange audit records show the victim's mailbox being read from 203.0.113.200 over three days, but `SigninLogs | where IPAddress == "203.0.113.200"` returns nothing, and every SigninLogs entry for the victim comes from the office. What best explains the empty result?

options.text: SigninLogs stores only failed sign-ins, so successful access from the attacker's address is never recorded there
IPAddress is a dynamic column, so an exact == comparison never matches and the filter has to use has instead
Token refreshes are non-interactive sign-ins, stored in AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs rather than SigninLogs
The workspace keeps SigninLogs for only 24 hours, so events older than a day have already aged out of the table

explanation.correct: SigninLogs holds interactive user sign-ins, where the user presents a factor. When a client uses a refresh token to obtain new access tokens, Entra ID logs a non-interactive sign-in, and Sentinel stores those in a separate table, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs. Access that lasts three days requires repeated token refreshes, so the attacker's IP should appear there. Hunt across both: `union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | where IPAddress == "203.0.113.200"`. If that table is empty too, check the Entra ID data connector: non-interactive sign-ins are a separate log type that has to be selected for streaming.

distractors.a: SigninLogs records both successes (ResultType 0) and failures.
distractors.b: IPAddress is a string column in SigninLogs, and == is a valid exact match.
distractors.d: Retention is set per workspace or table and is far longer than 24 hours by default.

explanation.interview_angle: Knowing where each kind of sign-in lands in the SIEM, so "no rows" is not mistaken for "no activity".

questions.question: A bank's investigators need to know who opened files in a credit-committee folder on file server FS-CREDIT last week. Its Security log has plenty of 4624 and 4634 events and "Audit File System" success auditing is enabled by Group Policy, yet there are no 4663 events for that folder. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: 4663 is written on the client workstation that opened the file, not on the file server that holds it
4663 records only failed access attempts, and every access to the folder last week succeeded
The folder has no SACL auditing entry for reads, and 4663 is only logged when the SACL asks for it
Audit Logon must also be set to log failures before any object access events can appear in the log

explanation.correct: Object access auditing needs two things: the audit subcategory (Audit File System) enabled, and a SACL on the folder or file with an auditing entry for the principals and access types of interest, such as Everyone / Read data. With only the policy set, Windows has nothing to audit on that folder, so no 4663 appears. This cannot be fixed retroactively, so last week's question must be answered from other sources (EDR file telemetry, 5145 events if "Audit Detailed File Share" was on, DLP logs), and a tightly scoped SACL should be added now for the rest of the investigation.

distractors.a: 4663 is logged on the computer where the object lives, here FS-CREDIT.
distractors.b: 4663 records access rights that were actually used and has no failure variant; failed handle requests appear as 4656 failures.
distractors.d: Audit Logon governs 4624 and 4625 logon events and has no effect on whether file access is audited.

explanation.interview_angle: Knowing that "auditing is enabled" in policy is not the same as the object being audited, before promising investigators a file-access timeline.

questions.question: A user's account is locked out every morning. On the domain controller you find event 4740 for that account. Which field tells you which computer sent the bad passwords?

options.text: Caller Computer Name
Subject: Account Name
Account That Was Locked Out: Security ID
Subject: Logon ID

explanation.correct: Caller Computer Name, under Additional Information, is the computer from which the logon attempt arrived that triggered the lockout. Common culprits are a phone or laptop with an old saved password, a mapped drive or scheduled task using stale credentials, or someone guessing. Go to that computer and look for the matching 4625 events or the stale credential. In the event XML this value sits in the TargetDomainName field, so parsed SIEM data often shows it under that name.

distractors.b: The Subject is the account that performed the lockout operation, normally the domain controller's own system account, not the source of the bad passwords.
distractors.c: This identifies the account that was locked out, which you already know.
distractors.d: Logon ID correlates events within one logon session; it does not name the source computer.

questions.question: An MSSP analyst gets a threat-intelligence hit: the client's perimeter firewall logged DNS queries for a known command-and-control domain, all with source 10.0.0.53, the client's internal DNS server. What is the right next step?

options.text: Isolate 10.0.0.53 from the network straight away, because it is the host that is talking to the C2 domain
Close the alert as a false positive, since DNS servers look up all kinds of domains on behalf of other systems
Block 10.0.0.53 from sending any DNS to the internet so that the C2 domain can no longer be resolved by anyone
Search the DNS server's own query logs, or endpoint DNS telemetry, to find which client asked

explanation.correct: A recursive resolver queries upstream on behalf of its clients, so every outbound lookup carries the resolver's own address. The firewall can only say that something inside asked; the endpoint that asked is in the resolver's own logs (on Windows DNS Server, the analytic or debug log; on other resolvers, query logging) or in EDR DNS events from the endpoints. Resolver query logging is often off by default, so if it is missing, use endpoint telemetry and advise the client to enable it. Once the client host is found, contain that host, and sinkhole or block the domain on the resolver.

distractors.a: Isolating the resolver breaks name resolution for the whole client and leaves the infected endpoint running.
distractors.b: A resolver looking up a known C2 domain means a client asked for it; the address is the resolver's, but the request is real.
distractors.c: This stops all internet name resolution for the client. Blocking or sinkholing the one domain on the resolver avoids the outage, and the infected host still has to be found.

explanation.interview_angle: Understanding that the source IP in an egress log is not always the culprit, and choosing proportionate containment.

questions.question: A threat hunter correlates risky sign-ins with mailbox rule creation using `RiskySignins | join (InboxRules) on UserPrincipalName`, without a kind= option. One user had six risky sign-ins from three IP addresses, but every joined row shows the same single sign-in. Why?

options.text: Without kind=, join behaves as leftanti and returns only part of the left table
The default flavour, innerunique, keeps one left row per key value before matching
The UserPrincipalName comparison is case-sensitive, so five of the sign-ins did not match
join keeps only the most recent left row per key, so the earlier sign-ins are dropped

explanation.correct: KQL's default join flavour is innerunique: it deduplicates the left side on the join key, keeping one arbitrary row per UserPrincipalName, and matches that row to every right-side row. For hunting this silently hides evidence; here five sign-ins and two of the three IPs disappear. Write `join kind=inner` whenever every left row matters, and put the smaller table on the left for performance. Splunk's join has its own trap (a limit on subsearch results), so in either tool compare joined output against the unjoined counts.

distractors.a: leftanti returns left rows with no match on the right, but this output does contain matches.
distractors.c: All six sign-ins belong to the same user with the same UPN string, so case is not what removed them.
distractors.d: innerunique keeps an arbitrary row, not the newest. If you want the latest sign-in, ask for it explicitly with arg_max().

explanation.interview_angle: Knowing which defaults silently drop rows; a hunter who does not will report fewer attacker IPs than were used.

questions.question: A rule alerts only on Event ID 1102. In a purple-team test, the operator runs `wevtutil cl System` and `wevtutil cl "Windows PowerShell"` on a server and the rule stays silent. Which TWO statements are correct? (Choose 2)

options.text: Clearing the System log also wipes any record of the clearing itself, so nothing is left to detect
Event ID 1102 is written only when the Security log is cleared, so clearing other logs does not trigger it
wevtutil cannot clear a log while the Windows Event Log service is running, so nothing was actually cleared
Event ID 4719 is logged for every cleared log and would be the better single event to alert on
Clearing System and other logs is recorded as Event ID 104 in the System log, which the rule should also cover

explanation.correct: 1102 ("The audit log was cleared") is specific to the Security log (b). When System, Application or another channel is cleared, Windows writes Event ID 104 from the Eventlog provider into the System log, after the clear, into the fresh log (e). A complete rule covers both: in Sentinel, `SecurityEvent | where EventID == 1102` plus `Event | where EventLog == "System" and EventID == 104`; in Splunk, `(source="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=1102) OR (source="WinEventLog:System" EventCode=104)`. Because events were forwarded before the clear, the SIEM still holds what the attacker tried to erase.

distractors.a: Event 104 is written into the newly cleared System log, and copies already forwarded to the SIEM are untouched.
distractors.c: wevtutil cl clears a live channel through the Event Log service; administrators use it routinely.
distractors.d: 4719 means the system audit policy was changed. It is worth alerting on too, but it is not logged when a log is cleared.

questions.question: A client's proxy alert flags a workstation sending large HTTPS POST requests to a cloud domain. Which TWO observations in the proxy logs most strengthen an exfiltration hypothesis? (Choose 2)

options.text: Across many sessions to the domain, bytes_out far exceeds bytes_in (3.2 GB out, 4 MB in)
The requests all received HTTP 200 responses from the destination server
The traffic went to destination port 443
The domain first appeared in the client's logs this week and only this host contacts it
The user agent string is a current version of a mainstream web browser such as Chrome or Edge

explanation.correct: Normal browsing downloads far more than it uploads, so a strongly upload-heavy byte ratio to one destination (a) is the core exfiltration signal, and a destination that is new to the whole organisation and used by a single host (d) makes a routine business explanation less likely. Next checks: what the domain is (newly registered, personal storage), who the user is (leaver, privileged), and which files the endpoint touched before the uploads. In KQL on CommonSecurityLog: `summarize Out = sum(SentBytes), In = sum(ReceivedBytes) by SourceIP, DestinationHostName`; in Splunk: `stats sum(bytes_out) as out sum(bytes_in) as in by src, dest`.

distractors.b: 200 is the normal success code for almost all web traffic, benign or malicious.
distractors.c: Port 443 carries nearly all web traffic, so it does not distinguish exfiltration.
distractors.e: A mainstream browser user agent is what normal traffic looks like; if anything, a script or unknown client would raise suspicion.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage

questions.question: Order these search stages so the result shows, per user and per hour, the upload volume in MB and keeps only hours above 500 MB.

options.text: | eval up_mb = round(up/1024/1024, 1)
| where up_mb > 500
index=proxy action=allowed http_method=POST
| stats sum(bytes_out) as up by _time, user
| bin _time span=1h

explanation.correct: The base search (c) comes first so only allowed POST events from the proxy index flow down the pipe. bin (e) rounds _time to the hour before aggregation, and stats (d) groups by _time and user, which is what makes the result hourly. eval (a) can only convert up to MB after stats has created it, and where (b) can only filter on up_mb after eval has created it. Each stage depends on a field the previous one produced, which is the rule for reading any SPL or KQL pipeline. The KQL shape is the same: `| summarize up = sum(SentBytes) by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h), SourceUserName | extend up_mb = round(up / 1024.0 / 1024.0, 1) | where up_mb > 500`.

questions.subtopic: Proxy and web server log fields
questions.question: Match each W3C extended log field, as used by web servers and proxies, to what it records.

left.text: cs-bytes
sc-bytes
cs-method
sc-status
cs-uri-stem

right.text: HTTP status code returned to the client
Bytes sent from the server back to the client, such as a downloaded file
Path requested, without the query string
Bytes the client sent to the server, such as an uploaded file
Time the request took to complete
HTTP verb the client used, such as GET or POST

explanation.correct: The prefix gives the direction: c is client, s is server, cs is client-to-server and sc is server-to-client. So cs-bytes counts what the client sent (the upload direction, the one to watch for exfiltration), sc-bytes what came back (the download direction), cs-method is the verb the client sent, sc-status the code the server returned, and cs-uri-stem the requested path without the query. The leftover description is time-taken. Proxy products often rename these fields (bytes_out, bytes_in, http_method, status), but the direction logic stays the same.

distractors.l1: Swapping cs-bytes and sc-bytes reverses upload and download; a "large upload" rule built on sc-bytes would flag big downloads instead.
distractors.l2: sc-bytes is server-to-client: large values are downloads, not data leaving the organisation.

left.text: stats count by user
eval
table
rename
fields - (remove the listed fields)

right.text: summarize count() by user
extend
project
project-rename
project-away
mv-expand

questions.subtopic: Linux privilege use in auth logs
questions.question: During a review of a bank's payment-gateway Linux server, match each auth log line to what it shows.

left.text: sshd[4120]: Accepted publickey for svc_batch from 10.12.0.40 port 50522 ssh2: ED25519 SHA256:Qm3x...
sshd[4188]: Failed password for invalid user oracle from 203.0.113.77 port 40112 ssh2
sudo:   deploy : TTY=pts/1 ; PWD=/home/deploy ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/cat /etc/shadow
su[5120]: pam_unix(su:session): session opened for user root(uid=0) by deploy(uid=1001)
sudo: pam_unix(sudo:auth): authentication failure; logname=deploy uid=1001 euid=0 tty=/dev/pts/1 ruser=deploy rhost=  user=deploy

right.text: deploy switched to a full root session with su
deploy ran one command as root through sudo, reading the password hash file
A successful SSH login authenticated with a key
deploy typed a wrong password at the sudo prompt
A password guess for a username that does not exist on this server
root logged in directly over SSH with a password

explanation.correct: "Accepted publickey" means key-based authentication succeeded (l1); "invalid user" marks a name that does not exist locally (l2). sudo writes one line per command it runs, with the invoking user first, the target user in USER= and the full command in COMMAND= (l3); reading /etc/shadow as root is a credential-access red flag on a payments server. su opening a session for root "by deploy" is a switch to an interactive root shell (l4), after which sudo logs nothing about the individual commands, so shell history or auditd becomes the evidence. A pam_unix "authentication failure" under the sudo service is a wrong password at the sudo prompt (l5). None of the lines shows a direct root SSH login, the leftover description.

distractors.l1: publickey, not password: mixing the two up hides whether password authentication is exposed on the server.
distractors.l4: This is su, not sudo: the user obtained a whole root shell, so do not expect per-command sudo lines afterwards.

explanation.interview_angle: Telling sudo from su in the logs, because it decides whether you have a command-level audit trail or have to find another one.
